title: Visa (V) Stock Faces Margin Squeeze Despite Strong Revenue Growth - simplywall.st
content:
Visa walked into this earnings print with its stock already up solidly over the past quarter, yet the immediate reaction was a shrug. The share price slipped about 0.7% to around US$366, even as the company posted another quarter of double digit net revenue and earnings growth. The headline this time is not payment volume; it is profitability. Net revenue reached US$11.6b while net income came in at US$5.6b, but trailing net profit margin has eased to 50.3%. Investors now have to weigh that slight margin squeeze against the still strong earnings engine behind Visa’s network. Is Visa’s premium 30x P/E simply the price of quality, or does it leave less room for error if growth cools from here? Bulls argue Visa’s core network plus value added services, cross border and stablecoin or AI projects can keep growth resilient even as traditional fees come under pressure. This quarter gives that view some real proof points. Net revenue grew 14% while payments volume and processed transactions each rose 10%, which confirms the core engine is still adding volume. The stronger data sits in the mix. Value added services revenue reached US$3.8b and rose 34%, with over 1,200 advisory projects and broad uptake of risk and issuing tools. Commercial and money movement revenue rose 17%, while Visa Direct transactions rose 21% to 4b. Management is also reallocating headcount savings into AI, agentic commerce and stablecoin platforms. That combination of higher margin services growth and reinvestment into new rails lines up with the bullish narrative rather than contradicting it. Bears focus on three issues for Visa: margin pressure from client incentives and opex, structural threats from alternative rails and rising regulatory or merchant pushback on fees. The quarter gives them some support but not a clear break in the story. Trailing net profit margin eased to 50.3% from 51.6% while operating expenses rose 17% and client incentives rose 18%. That shows pricing power is not unchecked and that growth is costing more to defend. At the same time, payments volume, cross border and commercial flows all rose at double digit rates and value added services grew faster than expenses. Stablecoin and agentic commerce work is framed as partnership rather than being bypassed. The print therefore confirms that profit density is a live pressure point but does not yet show the feared shift away from Visa’s rails in the reported numbers. title: F/V Odin crew revives deckhand with CPR after overboard near-drowning - Petersburg Pilot
content:

The Odin's crewman was hoisted into the Coast Guard search and rescue Jayhawk helicopter for quick transport to Mt. Edgecumbe Medical Center in Sitka on Sunday July 26, 2026. The Odin's crewman was hoisted into the Coast Guard search and rescue Jayhawk helicopter for quick transport to Mt. Edgecumbe Medical Center in Sitka on Sunday July 26, 2026. Trevor McKay pulls crewmate Tausani Ieremia from the water as Mike Doyle and Brent Birchell rush to haul him aboard the F/V Odin and commence the CPR that, after ten minutes, resuscitated him. On Wednesday, July 29, Trevor McKay, Mike Doyle, Brent Birchell and Mark Severson sent their encouragement to their fellow FV Odin crewman Tausani Ieremia at home in Sitka, recovering from the accident. Tausani Ieremia, of Sitka, was setting the net aboard the Petersburg seiner Odin on the morning of Sunday, July 26, when the boat's own purse line snared his ankle and dragged him over the stern and into the water near Saint Joseph Island, west of Prince of Wales. In the minutes that followed, the 22-year-old fisherman was pulled under by the net, lost consciousness and stopped breathing. The Odin's crew pulled him back, revived him with CPR. He was helicoptered by the Coast Guard to Sitka then life-flighted to Anchorage. He is now home recovering in Sitka. The accident happened around 11:30 a.m., skiffman Trevor McKay said. Fishing has been slow so far this season, and it was slow again that morning as the Odin began its set. Ieremia had just fixed a lead line and walked to the stern to throw it clear when he stepped into a bight of the purse line. It caught him by the ankle and pulled him over the stern - a moment captured on the boat's deck camera. Skipper Mark Severson was setting the net slowly, around two knots, and is glad he was, figuring that the low speed probably spared Ieremia much worse injury going over the stern. McKay, running the power skiff, had been watching the net go out. "I usually look at the net go out for the first 10 to 15 fathoms before I give it any gas," he said. The net was clear, so he turned and began to speed up toward the kelp line. "It wasn't long before I felt a big jerk," he said - usually the sign of a ring snarl. He looked back and saw "a body and a tangle of web flying over the rail." McKay released the pin as Severson immediately came over the radio - "Go get him!" - spun the skiff around and ran full throttle toward Ieremia. He watched him go down and surface once, then turned to ready his plunger pole. When he looked again, "all I could see was his hand, and it was sinking." He reached the net, threw the skiff in reverse and landed just above a set of sunken corks. Ieremia was nowhere in sight, pulled into the dark water by the weight of the fishing gear. Corks sit low like that only when something is tangled in the purse line or rings, McKay said. He swirled his pole through the water, hoping Ieremia might grab it. Nothing. Minutes passed. "I started to feel the reality that he isn't going to come back up," McKay said. Then there were bubbles, and a hand rose toward him through the sunlit water alongside the corks - "like an angel was guiding him up to me." Ieremia had managed to slip from his boots, freeing him from the net, said Severson. McKay caught Ieremia's hand and lifted him about halfway out of the water. "His eyes were as big as I've seen, lips blue and skin pale," he said. Ieremia was too heavy to pull in, and everything on his raingear McKay grabbed with his free hand was tearing or breaking; he held tightly onto Ieremia's hand. "I remember yelling, 'Help! I need help,'" he said. He felt the grip in Ieremia's hand fade to nothing; Ieremia's head fell back as he lost consciousness. The Odin was right on top of them by then, McKay said, and the crew got Ieremia up onto the deck and immediately started CPR. On the Odin's deck, crew members Mike Doyle and Brent Birchell began chest compressions and rescue breaths - McKay soon joined them. Water came up from his lungs from the chest compressions, Severson said. After around ten minutes of continuous CPR, Ieremia began breathing on his own. He grew more responsive over the next 20 minutes and was on his feet roughly a half-hour after that. "I was told to never stop CPR trying to save a life," McKay said. "We weren't going to stop." The F/V Reality, a nearby seiner with a crewmember trained as an EMT, reached the Odin soon after Ieremia had been revived and assisted with his care, the family told the Pilot. A Coast Guard Jayhawk helicopter crew arrived and lowered a rescue swimmer to the deck, and Ieremia got into the rescue basket under his own power, Severson said. The Coast Guard flew him to Mt. Edgecumbe Medical Center in Sitka; a Coast Guard public affairs officer said he was in stable condition when he was delivered. Guardian Flight then flew Tausani and his father, Joe, to Providence hospital in Anchorage for ICU monitoring. He thankfully had no broken ribs and no brain damage, Severson said, but was very bruised from the chest compressions; the family said the water remaining in his lungs was cleared in Anchorage. He is now home. Severson, who has fished for about 50 years, said he sets his net slowly by habit - so that if something goes wrong, the boat does less damage. In five decades, he said, he had never seen a crewman taken over the stern like that, "but always worried about it." Just two days before the accident, he remembers warning the crew: "Don't get close to the net and never turn your back on it." Severson said he hopes the near-miss pushes the whole seine fleet to tighten up around the net and to stay current on first aid. "Everybody needs to go do their CPR class every year," he said. It had been years since his own last class, he acknowledged, and techniques change - but what his crew did worked. He shared the deck-camera footage which captured the entire incident with the Coast Guard and his insurer, who praised the Odin's crew for their nonstop effort. "It was the most horrifying, worst set of my life, and it turned out to be the best one," Severson said. He knew Ieremia would be all right, he said, when the young fisherman got to his feet on deck. "He's a great kid," he said. In their statement, the Ieremia family thanked McKay, Doyle, Birchell and Severson, the crew of the F/V Reality, the neighboring boats, the Coast Guard and the Guardian Flight crew that carried their son to Anchorage. They singled out "the incredible skill and herculean effort taken by Trevor to retrieve him and never let go," Severson's handling of the boat around the net "under intense pressure," and Doyle and Birchell, "who performed CPR and didn't stop." "Tausani is now home, surrounded by family and friends, as he recovers from the injuries and trauma of this near-tragic fishing accident," the family wrote. "We all know how amazing it is that we have this incredible outcome of Tausani's survival. It feels like a miracle." Powered by ROAR Online Publication Software from Lions Light Corporation

title: 'A Genuine BMW M3 Threat At A Hefty Discount' - The Cadillac ATS-V Is A Used Bargain Masterpiece - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update When it comes to securing yourself some sort of practical performance coupe or sedan, there are excellent options from all over the world. Creations cooked up by the likes of Audi, BMW, and Mercedes-Benz illustrate Germany's effectiveness in the sector, while other European options are available from manufacturers like Alfa Romeo and Jaguar. Then you have more reliable and affordable models from Korean and Japanese brands, before you inevitably get to American machinery. Cadillac has pushed hard to increase its performance range in the last couple of decades, and now one of its earlier attempts is an absolute used bargain. During the 2010s, Cadillac started to raise its ambitions to take the fight directly to sports coupe and sedan experts like BMW and Mercedes-Benz, having previously focused on building cut-price alternatives for those who wanted performance for significantly less. Cadillac's pedigree was of ultra-luxury and peak excellence though, as opposed to a budget version of premium European machines, so the decision was taken to aim squarely at its foreign rivals going forward. The ATS-V is a perfect illustration of this refreshed approach, with the model being the performance version of the ATS, Cadillac's compact executive coupe and sedan that was designed to go up against cars like BMW's 3 and 4 Series ranges. As a result, the V was developed to take on the M3 and M4 at their own game. The ATS-V was thus available in both two-door coupe and four-door sedan forms, to take on the equivalent M4 and M3 offerings, respectively. Thus, the ATS-V was born with sporting pretensions from the start, built upon GM's Alpha platform. Yep, the very same foundations used by the Chevrolet Camaro muscle car. When combining performance and usability, beating BMW's phenomenal M3 and M4 models is the benchmark every manufacturer looking to get involved in the battle had to aim for. From a power standpoint, the Caddy came out of the blocks swinging. While BMW's creations used a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six engine, the ATS-V utilized a larger 3.6-liter twin-turbo V6, which pumped out just shy of 40 horsepower more than the BMWs could manage. That wasn't all, as the Cadillac's V6 also provided its driver with an extra 40 lb-ft of torque, an important benefit considering the Caddy tipped the scales at just under 300 pounds heavier in either form. The extra firepower more than made up for the extra mass, as both the ATS-V coupe and sedan could sprint to 60 mph in 3.8 seconds, while the BMW competitors had to settle for a 4.1-second dash. As a tradeoff, you'd expect the BMWs to take control once you got to the bends, but don't be so sure. While the suspension used on the M cars made for a more composed and usable handling balance on rougher roads, the ATS-V's excellent electronic setup and finely tuned chassis really came into their own on smoother routes. The extra grunt adds some extra spice to proceedings, while its powerful Brembo braking system matches up well to the BMW's own setup. The ATS-V squared up surprisingly effectively with the M3 and M4, but expect to work harder to extract its potential unless you have access to a silky-smooth racetrack. As with the M3 and M4, the beauty of the ATS-V is that, depending on your circumstances, you have a couple of different body style options. Should you not have kids or any rear passengers to worry about, the coupe provides a sleeker exterior design that arguably stands out better on the road than the sedan variant. Plus, due to lacking a couple of rear doors, it's also a little lighter overall. It also retains the same size trunk and legroom as the sedan, since the two cars are built on an identical chassis. The sedan makes sense for those who have a family to transport, since it has a useful pair of rear doors so that you can access the rear compartment more easily. That makes it more straightforward to strap your children into their travel seats, not to mention accessing the rear seats should you want to fold them down to fit larger objects in the trunk. Plus, the sedan's less streamlined silhouette promotes extra headroom out front, to the tune of an inch. Rear headroom is the same as the coupe, since both cars feature the same sloping roofline towards the back. Notably, taller drivers may find the extra headspace of the sedan more comfortable, so it's worth sitting in both vehicles before you decide. While the ATS-V's effectiveness as a performance car against the likes of the M3 and M4 is impressive, that's nothing when you consider just how cheap they are these days. In their last years of production, 2018 for the sedan and 2019 for the coupe, they demanded $61,595 and $67,795, respectively, prices that were around $1k and $5k cheaper than their equivalent BMW M rivals. This proved decent value at the time, but Cadillac's relative lack of pedigree versus the legendary BMW M name has seen both models plunge in value in the years since. Tidy examples of either car can be had for as little as $20k these days, though these will be higher mileage with less meat left on the bone. On average, you'll need to spend around $33,400 to net yourself a clean sedan ATS-V with around 60,000 miles on the clock, while an equivalent coupe specimen will set you back around a grand more. If you want to purchase a used M3 or M4 of similar age and mileage, you'll have to lay down well over $40k, and in the case of the former, closer to $50k. In fact, a used 2023 BMW 330i has the same sort of average value as the ATS-V, which provides much less in the way of performance and creature comforts for a car that's only a few years younger. The ATS-V's used market performance was always going to be weaker than the M3 or M4, since BMW's M heritage proves to be a greater pull for most gearheads than Cadillac's reputation for primarily offering soft luxury cars for an older demographic. It is doing a good job of changing this, so expect more modern models to fare better in this regard. As far as the ATS-V goes, just be thankful that you can secure yourself a genuine BMW M3/M4 threat at a hefty discount. The beauty of the ATS-V featuring a Cadillac badge is that, along with the BMW M-challenging performance, it's also a damn nice place to be. Its power-adjustable, half leather and half suede microfiber seats provide great comfort and support, making them ideal for both cruising along a highway and exploring the limits of the ATS-V's engaging chassis. They are heated too, which helps make those cold winter mornings that little bit less intimidating. There's also an eight-inch touchscreen infotainment setup with the usual Apple CarPlay and Android Auto capability, a premium sound system, as well as convenient climate and cruise control, as you'd expect with a higher-end model. When looking for used examples, be sure to seek out the optional Recaro sports seats, as they turn the comfort and support dial up a notch, and are well worth having. That said, don't expect the cabin to feel as premium as its German rivals, primarily as the materials are similar to those used in the standard ATS. They look and feel cheaper than the materials found in the M3/M4, which is a little disappointing given how close in price they were when new. With the decent discount you get with used examples in 2026 though, this setback can perhaps be a little easier to swallow. Despite having a slightly subpar cabin, the ATS-V makes up for it with its engaging driving experience. It is not only genuinely fun to drive, but being able to blast past the 0-60 mph barrier in under four seconds for less than $30k is genuinely compelling. The fact that it can be legitimately mentioned in the same breath as the M3/M4 as far as driving dynamics are concerned tells you everything you need to know about this bargain sports sedan. title: Gen. V Homes celebrates 6th anniversary - Post and Courier
content: Generation V (five) Homes is celebrating six years of helping Lowcountry families build custom homes on their own land, marking a milestone for the family-owned company that has grown into one of the region's leading modular home builders. Founded in July 2020, Generation V Homes combines five generations of homebuilding experience with a full-service approach to modular construction. Since opening its doors on Johns Island, the company has worked with homeowners throughout Charleston, Beaufort, Hilton Head, Georgetown, Orangeburg and surrounding communities to design and build custom homes tailored to each family's property, lifestyle and budget. Unlike many builders that focus on planned developments, Generation V Homes specializes in building on client-owned land and managing the entire construction process from start to finish — trees to keys. Their turnkey services include permitting, site preparation, land clearing, well and septic systems, driveway installation, site-specific engineering, site-built additions, comprehensive project management and final construction required to deliver a completed home. Generation V Homes is the only true full-service modular builder in the region. Backed by years of experience building custom homes, the team can transform a modular home into a truly one-of-a-kind residence with personalized layouts, finishes and design features that reflect each homeowner's vision. "Reaching six years in business is an exciting milestone for our entire team," said Jim Picha, Sales Manager of Generation V Homes. "We're grateful to every homeowner who has trusted us with one of the biggest investments they'll ever make. Every home we build is unique, and we're proud to continue serving families throughout the Lowcountry with the same commitment to quality and personal service that has guided our family for generations." The anniversary comes as demand for build-on-your-lot homes continues to grow across coastal South Carolina. More homeowners are choosing to build on family land or property they already own, creating opportunities for customized homes outside of traditional subdivisions. From affordable modular designs to fully custom two-story homes, Generation V Homes combines the efficiency of modular construction with decades of custom homebuilding expertise, allowing homeowners to create a home that is truly their own. As Generation V Homes looks to the future, its commitment remains the same: delivering high-quality, custom homes that empower families to build where and how they want — without compromise. title: Anthropic v. U.S. Department of War: A Hearing Diary - Lawfare
content:
The upcoming main navigation can be gotten through utilizing the tab key. Any buttons that open a sub navigation can be triggered by the space or enter key. On July 30, U.S. District Judge Rita Lin of the Northern District of California held a hearing on cross-motions for summary judgment in Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War. In the suit, Anthropic is challenging the Department of Defense’s unprecedented designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk last March under 10 U.S.C. § 3252. The dispute arose out of Anthropic’s refusal to permit the government to use its frontier artificial intelligence products for lethal autonomous weapons or mass surveillance of the U.S. population. Anthropic alleges that the designation was unconstitutional punishment for First Amendment protected speech and also violated its Fifth Amendment Due Process rights and the Administrative Procedure Act. The government alleges that its actions were justified by legitimate national security concerns that grew out of distrust of the company and concern that undisclosed guardrails, built into its products to effectuate the company’s private view of morality, could risk the safety of warfighters and civilians. Last March, Judge Lin granted a preliminary injunction in favor of Anthropic. The parties agree that the case is now ready for final decision on the merits on the basis of the written record. (Anthropic has a similar suit pending against the Defense Department in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to challenge a supply-chain risk designation Secretary Pete Hegseth made at about the same time under a different statute: 41 U.S.C. § 4713.) Lawfare’s Roger Parloff live-posted the hearing as it happened, by following on a Zoom feed. Read his account by clicking the button below or by viewing his thread on X here. At 1pm ET / 10 am PT Judge Rita Lin (NDCal) will be holding a hearing in @Anthropic v. @Department of War 🇺🇸 [sic]. It's on cross-motions for summary judgment, meaning each side seeks a final decision on the merits based on papers. I’ll try to live-post for @Lawfare …
            /1 Anthropic is seeking a permanent injunction to stop the DOD's designation of it as a "supply chain risk." It alleges that the declaration was to punish it for 1st Amendment protected speech, among other claims. Judge Lin issued a preliminary injunction earlier. ... /2 Judge Lin issued a list of 5 questions she wants to the attys to be prepared to answer. She will likely ask them to address those first. You can find those here: https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.465515/gov.uscourts.cand.465515.242.0.pdf  ... /3 Anthropic filed 2 cases, because the DOD invoked two "supply chain risk" statutes. The NDCal case (today's hearing) stems from 10 USC 3252. A parallel case relating to 41 USC 4713 is pending in the DC Circuit, where that statute requires those claims to be brought. ... /4 I am listening to a Zoom hookup, which the NDCal allows. They're getting the judge now. /5 All rise.
                [Just audio, no video.]
                Counsel are giving appearances.
                Plaintiff's lead: MIchael Mongan from @WilmerHale ...
                DOJ: James Harlow with Christian Dibblee.
                /6 Judge Lin wants to start with some of her impressions than go her questions. She'll reserve time for attys to bring up other matters.
                having reviewed the record it appears to me to be largely the same as record i assessed at prelim injunction stage. dont see additional

                /7 evidence from govt that [improves] their position. if anything it's gotten worse.
                don't see any nefarious signs ...
                Anthropic criticized DOW's positions in the press. and that created "a lack of trust," per govt. govt saying if contractor criticizes govt, govt can turn around
                /8 and say we dont trust you and govt can go ahead and retaliate, say they're an enemy of the state, taking away their contracts ... etc. Really troubling. at odds with 1st Am, with 3252. would like to understand if that's really govt's position. cause it seems quite extreme.
                /9 if that's not govt's position, want to know [how govt sees it].
                let's go thru more fine grain questions i have.
                start with Q1.
                /10 [she's reading the question now. It's about the pickering framework.] does it really apply when govt goes beyond terminating contactual relationship. 2d part of questions is a hypo to illustrate [my point]. ...
            /11 DOJ (Harlow): it depends on nature of hypothetical punishment. that comes from Umbehr. ... fact-intensive inquiry. Pickering is correct framework to apply. If govt is exercising more general regulatory power, Pickering would not apply. Our case: govt has acted as contractor. /12 Judge: one question i have. you use term regulatory. Not quite term Umbehr uses. it uses sovereign power. do you see govt conduct that attempts to deter on broader scope than just individual contractor by deterring from public criticism -- you see that as regulatory? /13 DOJ: by terminating a contract, you could see that as pressuring a company, but that's squarely within Umbehr. Judge: but govt is out there saying this is a warning to all of you, we're making public example of this company. you should never criticize govt in this way. ... /14 J: you think Pickering is correct framework? DOJ: yes, YH J: even if purpose is deter a broader swath of people watching? DOJ: ... if govt's messaging is directed to other contractors--remains withiin pickering. /15 Judge: so, the secondary boycott in this case--any defense contractor who does business with Anthropic would have contract terminated ... if that were still in effect -- beyond pickering? DOJ: no longer in case, but if it were across the board [like that] ... that's getting more into regulatory framework. /16 Judge Lin now referring to Hegseth's original declaration, which imposed a secondary boycott--would that go beyond pickering? DOJ Harlow: to extent action govt took had no nexus to any govt contract Judge: so if Hegseth's original had come into force ... DOJ Harlow: if it's unrelated to a covered system, how to see how Pickering would apply /17 Judge: suppose it was implemented just as Hegseth originally said ... nobody can conduct commercial activity with Anthropic ... DOJ: can't give a categorical answer. 3252 applies to all covered procurement actions. we dont need to speculate. we know secy's social media statement was reduced. he has no legal authority beyond the covered procurement actions in the statute. /18 Judge: suppose contractor is terminated becausae they did unrelated work with Anthropic ... Pickering would not apply, would you agree? DOJ: it wouldn't be that 3d party contractor bringing the claim. if contract entirely unrelated to covered systems of DOW, the case law doesn't appear to have extended pickering to that situation. /19 [Pickering is a doctrine that permits the govt to have more leeway to constrain speech when govt is an employer constraining speech of an employee or independent contractor.] /20 Judge: if govt said ... reason we're doing this is to stop unfair criticism of the president. does pickering apply? DOJ: yes. Umbehr & Pickering are equipped to handle that sort of scenario. The govt has to prove that it has a legitimate govt business. /21 Judge: so one could use Pickering framework and still violate 1st Amendment in that case? DOJ: [implies that that's right]. that's not this case. Judge: i'm surprised you can't give a yes to what seems to be an easy case. DOJ: i've given best answer i can. in contrast to national security interest we've raised here, if it is just a pure, we dont like any criticism whatsoever, SCOTUS hasn't recognized that as legitimate interest. dont want to foreclose any hypothetical argument. /22 J: what if in my hypo, govt is announcing it's terminating all defense contracts of anhyone who has ever criticized the president. ... chilling effect ... govt says reason we did this is because we can't trust you. now that you criticized president you might be anti-american. pickerign still applies? DOJ: correct. /23 J: would there be a violation of the 1st Am DOJ: it depends what facts govt can present to justify its position. Here, we think record amply demonstrates why Secy reached conclusion that facts justify a "supply chain risk" [designation]. not mere loss of trust here. /24 J: suppose added to billboard: nobody better do business with this company or else--pickering would not apply? DOJ: veering more toward exercise of sovereign or regulatory power J: i look at holistic sum total of govt's conduct . the hegseth directive. the presidential directive. then the formal designation. /26 DOJ: there would be a 1st Am analysis for P's post. 1st Am analysis for Secy's analysis. (we view as only the 3/3 letter, not the february post.) J: but assessing each challenged actdion, i need to look at context of what govt is doing as a whole, right? DOJ: each govt actor has different powers. POTUS has powers Secy does not [have]. /27 DOJ: there's a tendancy to lump all the defendants together. but each defendant operates in discrete authorities. not a monolith. J: i dont see a record made by President about the threat Anthropic posed. i can't consider what DOW knew and thought? DOJ: the record evidence as of date of POTUS's Truth Social post on 2/27. /28 J: doesn't look there's any info in record as of 2/27 about whether Anthropic posed a threat. DOJ: the DOW docs ... J: how do I know President saw that? DOJ: just evaluate on face of his Truth Social post. the parties agree that the record is the record. /29 J: i'll give plaintiffs an opp to respond. Michael Mongan: we have material dlifferences of opinion as to how pickering frameowrk operates. as to 1a, pickering applies when there's an employer/empoyee relationship or something closely analogous and challenged action is normal day-to-day action ... /30 MM: doesn't apply to all govt contractors or all actions taken to retaliate against [one]. terminating a contract could be like firing someone for cause. but it doesn't extend to exercises of sovereign power. here, pickering doesn't apply becauase providing frontier AI to DOW is not remotely analogous to anything an employee would do. /31 Plus, actions we challenge here are not similar to day to day managmeent of employees. they are classic exercises of sovereign power. this is not ordinary contracting to manage efficiency of public services and make sure there's order in teh workplace. easy to answer the question in this case. there's a whole body of law that addresses procurement. /32 if you want to ask what an employer would ordinarily do, turn to the procurement laws. ... that's not what they did here. each of challenged actions is classic exercise of sovereign power. the secondary boycott is still out there. X post is still out there in the public record. says no contractors can do business with Anthropoic without [consequences]. immediate debarment of Anthropic is exercise of sovereign power. /33 MM: even the exercise of 10 usc 3252 is unprecedented exercise of national security authority affecting all covered systems. some staggering implications to answer you just heard about the hypo. the govt could come out and say any contractor who criticizes fed govt is subject to punitive actions and that would be subject to pickering balancing would lead to immediate diminishing of their 1st Amendment rights. /34 MM: the reason you're not getting clear answers from the opposing lawyer is he's a good lawyer and realize those hypos may very well be the next case. our view--even if you apply pickering, our 1st Am claim would prevail. J: what is your view on how i look at 1st Am claims. look at actions as a whole to determine whether they were to retaliate--all 3 actions together. but govt says i should separate them out and look at separately. /35 MM: i don't see how you can separate them out on this record. POTUS post 2/27. Secy's post is a few hours later. Follow-on actions a few days later. all of these are entangled. makes sense to look at big picture. but even if you looked at them individually, answer is same. all violate 1st Am. /36 Judge moves to Q2. would it eviscerate 1st Am protections. ... DOJ: Pickering framework more than adequate to address this situation. plaintiff makes prima facie case, then burden shifts to govt to show its interest outweighs 1st Am interests. not simply about pubic criticism of DOW--lot more going on. /37 DOJ Harlow: what's happening here, dealing with frontier AI tech, which is a bit of a black box. opaque by its very nature. not like procuring a rifle. you can dissemble a rifle and make sure it's produced to your specs. not the case with frontier AI products. Anthropic also has privileged access to these models. /38 DOJ: nothing prevents Anthropic from deeloping new policy positions and baking them in with guardrails which may or may not be disclosed to DOW. DOW needs to trust AI vendors to be forthright and about what guardrails have been installed. J: so you're saying, okay for govt to say a contractor is a potential subversive because he can't be trusted -- fine & supportable in AI context? DOJ: not solely. there need to be articulable facts for why the trust is lost. this is laid out in undersecy michael's memo. /39 DOJ: but risk is much greater with AI than with ordinary hardware. Also, not a onetime transaction. With AI, dept needs access to latest AI models. to update it is not like doing software match. it has to be installed on system. each new update is new opportunity--need to think, has there been a new guardrail slipped into this model? /40 J: Is that really so diffefrent from other defense contractors. Drones ... each shipment could be different. is there a software component slipped in that could cause it to self-destruct? DOJ: AI is fundamentally different--not just from physical hardware--but even from traditional software. nature of these models is staggeringly enormous and opaque, dept can't peek beneath the hood and evaluate it in same way as with hardware. /41 J: what are articulable facts? DOJ: risk of AI poisoning. Undersecy applied risk framework. sum of whole is greater than each of the parts. parts secy identified: refusal of Anthropic to permit all lawful uses. dept never asked anthropic to produce a special model. dept wants to use the product wihtout external limitations Anthropic would impose upon it. /42 DOJ: a high level Anthropic official questioned use of a product during a military operation ... outreach ... why would you ask the question? J: what was teh question. not explained in the materials. DOJ: not suitable for public recrod. about ongoing active military operations. questioning propriety of the use. whether right for Anthropic's tech to be used for this ongoing operation. /43 J: do you think record precludes possibility that question was, "is it a good idea to use the product in this situation?" DOJ: yes. The prime contractor also grew concerned by the mere asking of the question. not within the purview of any company exec to question how & why its tech is being used. that gets to a "corporate moral judgment" that may be baked into a future version of the model. /44 J: so your articulable facts are contractual refusal and then the questioning? DOJ: and then ... undersecy had questions about safeguarding classified details. Anthropic raised the dispute -- the contract negotiations -- in late feb that Anthropic disclosed the nature of these to the public. said it was being threatened by DOW. directive within the company that expressed hostility to current DOW leadership. permissible under 1st Am case law--speech can be viewed as evidence of intent. all goes into the mix--does this company see itself as a partner or, in terms of 3252, the adversary supply-chain relationship. /45 DOJ: there should be deference to these officials. it's secy who bears ultimate responsibility for safeguarding nat sec systems. J: plaintiffs? Michael Mongan: So Q2 ... it would certainly violate 1st Am. we've addressed in briefing. explanations have evolved and shifted during this litigation. now this focus on trust. /46 MM: glad to hear DOJ acknowledge they need to point to specific articulable findings ... my colleague points to undersecy's risk analysis memo of 3/2. note that work on risk analysis memo took place after the directives of 2/27. setting that aside, heard a lot about the nature of frontier AI. perhaps more opaque. developer has privileged access. true of all frontier AI companies. has to be more than that. resist notion that because of these features, it's so different that 1st Am safeguards are radically different. /47 MM: what are articulable facts supposedly limited to Anthropic. "refusal to permit all lawful uses." the two anthropic specified have always been specified. govt knew that. so hard to swallow, all of a sudden on 2/27, this elevated the situation from contract [dispute] to supply chain risk. speaking with the press is a core 1st Am protected activity. you may not like contractor. may decide not to contract with them. doesn't make them supply chain risk. speaking publicly of great public significance--like AI safety and responsible use of your own models--creates situation where you are a supply chain risk and sanctioned by govt. /48 MM: question about use of Claude in a foreign situation. assume it's correct. doesn't remotely take you to conclusion that anthropic is an adversary bent on [undermining goals of govt]. question at issue was raised by one Anthropic exec to a 3d party. no evidence nobody took step to interfere in ongoing operation. Anthropic's CEO made clear not concern with foreign operations. Anthr went to meet with Hegseth in person, assured him we had no interest in interfering in those oeprations. and made clear they wouldn't in contract. /49 MM: if assuming a saboteur who is an adversary of the US--the last thing that person would do would make a principled stand about the importance of particular usage restrictions in terms of safety and responsible use. they'd just go ahead and promise anything and go ahead adn do their sabotage. /50 MM: heard my colleague say this is about pre-deployment model control. but that was not key thing in risk-analysis memo. concern was post-deployment. only once we made clear anthropic has no post-deployment control, did they pivot and start to focus on pre-deployment model control. that shifting of rationales is powerful evidence of pretext. problem for them both with respect to 1st Am and APA claim. /51 J: let me move to Q3. DOJ Harlow: we're not entirely sure what prompted this question. agencies' conduct beyond scope ... but to answer it ... the dept of war continues to wind down use of Anthropic products. process remains ongoing. scheduled to be completed by 9/30. /52 DOJ: there's a fair amount of nuance with respect to each agency's relationship to Anthropic. several using on pilot basis, winding down by August. fed govt dipping its toe into AI. exploring what tools are out there. agencies often using them thru 3d party vendors. /53 J: i hear you sahying DOW is winding down and will be done 9/30. DOJ: right J: most agencies still using? DOJ: preexisting pilots ... agencies have continued to carry out pilot programs. already slated to expire 8/30. J: Question 4: have any expanded use of Claude? /54 DOJ: defendants very respectfully object to this question. calls for confidential info ... calls for govt wide info about nat sec tools in this setting. also calls for conduct that post-dates agency action. outside record, not before def agencies. J: if true that DOW believes Anthropic to be nat sec threat that going to poison AI model, seems inconsistent for DOW to be, as reported, to be using Anthropic and expanding its use of teh AI model. doesn't that seem relevant at least to 1st Am claim? DOJ: any subsequent actions--Mythos model--not reflected in administrative record ... /55 J: sometimes someone's actions after the conduct in question give insight into their intent? DOJ: i appreciate that. i'm not authorized to give a substantive response today, but it might be possible for parties to meet and confer and for us to submit something afterwards. need to be careful about what we're providing and how. /56 J: plaintiffs? Michael Mongan: start with Q4. i hear govt saying this calls for sensitive info. maintaining strong relationship with govt is important to anthropic. we do think this is relevant for reasons YH indicated. that said, Anthropic's main priority is final judgment that will provide full relief against these unprecedented actions. if court interested in pursuing further, suggest we speak in camera ... maybe short filing tomorrow. but we'd hope that any further discussions would not delay the court in resolving this motion. /57 MM: regarding Question 3. most agencies have continued to work with Anthropic. 2 have paused contracts. we're not aware of any that have canceled any since preliminary injunction. we have limited info about extent to which agencies are "winding down" use. only 2d hand info. /58 J: my last question--this one for Anthropic: shouldn't any remedy also include a remand to allow DOW to attempt to make lawful [revision]? MM: default remedy which agency action is found unlawful--vacate and remand to agency. as practical matter, no viable way for DOW to lawfully designate Anthropic a supply chain risk on remand. as formal matter, we wouldn 't object tho. On 2d part ... agree no remand as to secondary boycott. DOj acknowledges no authority to do what he tried to do there. DOJ: as we argued, if inadequacies in 3252, this case is a prime candidate for remand without vacatur. DOW likely to remedy any deficiencies or procedural oversights and reach same decision. /59 DOJ: if court does invalidate the 3/3 order, we don't think you need a remand. as to secondary boycott, we dont see any -- if court would like secy to clarify whether secondary boycott exists -- remand without vacatur would bge appropriate. but if court is going to vacate 2/27 post, remand doesn't matter. /60 Michael Mongan (for plaintiffs): regarding remanding without vacatur ... not appropriate for situations with serious errors. can't imagine more serious errors than here. DOJ: want to offer rebuttal on some points. ... whether govt has exercised sovereign powers ... sovereign is imprecise. everything govt does is sovereign. really it's about regulatory work. /61 DOJ: for Q2, i forgot ... an additional risk factor. the CDC example. DOW has pointed to as demonstrated how it might manifest. J: but that was, they were using commercial model. it had restrictions. DOJ: but it demonstrates, there was a guardrail. ... CDC tried to use for permitted use, but it wouldn't because of a guardrail. that's what DOW fears. in a scenario where warfighters & civilians safety could be at risk. /62 DOJ: Mr. Mongan mentioned ... fact that DOW knew Anthropic's pre-existing statements about safety ... yes, but that favors us. nevertheless, DOW continued to work with the company. not just about company's speech. it was about additional factors i went through. On Question 4 ... Mr. Mongan asked for response by today or tomorrow. I would ask for week. just given nature of info sought and all the agencies. would take a lot of work to hash out a response. /63 DOJ: none of questions touched on due process or ultra vires J: i thought it was well briefed and i dont have questions DOJ: as to APA claim -- [Admininstrative Procedure Act] ... Anthropic had burden to put forward ... J: if something Anthropic said about actions of agencies that wasn't accurate, [say so]-- DOJ: a number of these agencies didn't have direct contract relationships with Anthropic. they have contract with 3d party cloud provider that has whole bunch of options, including use of Claude. ... shouldn't have judicial review of these work-a-day IP decisions. /64 DOJ: given some of Anthropic's concessions, seems that at least some defs are entitled to summary judgment. At least the EOP, the social sec administration, NEA, Does 1-10. Proposed order lumps together various actions and defendants; i think that's inappropriate. If court is going to find for Anthropic on any of the APA claims, court has to decide if equitable relief is warranted. we dont think so. /65 DOJ: but if court disagrees, important to tailor equitable relief to particular defendants. ... Also, any order should preserve right of agencies to stop using Anthropic. to extent these are ordinary procurement decisions, agencies have right to terminate contracts without cause. Also no basis for the compliance report included in the proposed order. no question of defendants' compliance with the preliminary injunction order. /66 Michael Mongan responding, for Anthropic: On Pickering, if govt exercises ordinary procurement authority, that could fall within Pickering. but here POTUS goes beyond that to just debarment, and secy following up, that very readily falls into sovereign, regulatory power. /67 MM: on question of MM: all AI models have guardrails. in CDC, it was using commercial model. we built govt model [to prevent this problem.] On Q4 ... govt had this question since Monday. timing does matter. we've been laboring under unc'l orders since February. campaign of retaliation. important to company to have final judgment that will provide us with relief expeditiously. Overarching point: separation of powers. Step back, suggestion seems to be there's no way for entitty to get any review of a presidential directive that concededly is not exercising any statutory authority and violates 1st Am and Due Process. That can't be right. /68 MM: we appreciate court and defs moving quickly. these are actions that profoundly harm anthropic and threaten to chill debate. Judge: I'll will take the matter under submission and issue a written order Adjourned. ... /69

title: Argenta Contemporary Theatre v. Stage 13 legal battle resolved - arktimes.com
content:
Arkansas news, politics, opinion, restaurants, music, movies and art A lawsuit filed by the Argenta Contemporary Theatre against several of its former staff members has reached a conclusion. According to a press release shared by ACT, the suit was resolved on Tuesday, when it was decided that Stage 13, a competing theater company formed by the ex-employees, will pay $150,000 to ACT. “Additionally, the Stage 13 defendants and William Feland are voluntarily dismissing their claims against ACT, Christian Gwatney Baker, and Vincent Insalaco,” the statement continues. “The settlement includes no confidentiality provision, and the litigation concludes without any finding or admission of wrongdoing by ACT or its leadership, all of whom consistently and categorically denied the allegations made against them from the outset.” Per a release from Stage 13, the settlement “includes no admission of liability or wrongdoing.” Their release also states that an anonymous donor provided “$150,000 to cover the settlement amount and personally paid all legal expenses.” The drama leading up to the lawsuit began on August 24, when a group of 13 employees at ACT abruptly resigned, quickly forming a new theater arts nonprofit called Stage 13. Soon after, ACT issued a release carrying some serious accusations: “In the midst of their sudden departure, ACT has learned of several alarming actions taken against its computer systems, intellectual property, and operations, including the unauthorized access and wiping of computers, deletion of website content, and the dissemination of false information regarding ACT’s upcoming educational programs.” Days later, ACT sued Stage 13, with the legal complaint referring to the situation as “one of the most brazen acts of corporate sabotage and betrayal imaginable in Arkansas’s nonprofit arts community.” A significant portion of the complaint against Stage 13 was devoted to accusations that the new group was trying to divert students enrolled in ACT’s educational programs to their own classes. In response, Stage 13 shared a statement of their own: “While at Argenta Contemporary Theatre, we reported and documented what we believed to be instances of misconduct that threatened the well-being and integrity of our staff, the people we serve, and the organization. Upon formally conveying our concerns, the situation escalated to the point that current ACT Board Chairman, Jeremy Ables, stated that he was not able to guarantee our personal safety and, that if he was in our position, he would leave and start a new company.” A counterclaim from Stage 13 eventually came in November, alleging a toxic work environment led by co-founder Vincent Insalaco that made them “feel uncomfortable, distressed, underappreciated, and concerned for the well-being of their students.” The counterclaim also expressed concerns about financial mismanagement. Around the same time, ACT and Insalaca were accused in a separate lawsuit of misrepresenting the use of hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of donations from a single donor — William Feland of Pinnacle Structures Inc. The suit was dismissed in May. Mrs. Donna Marie Pinney Lawrence, age 70, of Alston, died Wednesday, July 29, 2026, at Oxley Park & Rehab in Lyons following an extended illness. She was born near Boston Massachusetts on June 4, 1956, to the late Brace Pinney and Pauline Elisabeth Jenkins Pinney. She lived in Massachusetts until moving as a young teenager to Morrow, Georgia. She graduated in 1974 from Morrow High School in Clayton County and later worked with Southern Bell in Atlanta. She attended Swainsboro Tech, Brewton-Parker College in Mt. Vernon, and earned a Bachelor’s of Science Degree in Nursing from Clayton State. She worked as a register nurse at Meadows Memorial in Vidalia, Henry Medical in Stockbridge, and work in home healthcare in the Atlanta area for many years. She moved to Montgomery County in 2021; and she enjoyed crafts, especially scrapbooking and crocheting. In addition to her parents, she is preceded in death by three sisters, Pam Pinney Askew, Debra Pinney Harrington, and infant sister, Judith Ann Pinney; and one brother, Wayne Pinney. She is survived by her husband of forty-one years, Harold E. Lawrence of Alston; four children, Jon-Michael Carpenter and wife Jessica of Uvalda, Michael Lawrence and wife Lisa of Jesup, Luann Lawrence and Steven of Covington, and Shannon Marie Mayfield and husband Ben of Forsyth; one brother, Mark Pinney and wife Kitty of St. Joe, Florida; fourteen grandchildren, and numerous nieces and nephews. The funeral service will be held on Saturday morning, August 1, 2026, at 11:00 in the chapel of Ronald V. Hall Funeral Home with Reverend Josh Moran officiating. Interment will follow at Walker Cemetery near Alston. The family will receive friends at the funeral home on Saturday morning from 10:00 until just prior to the service. Flowers are welcome, or memorial donations may be made to Shriners Hospitals for Children by visiting their website at shrinerschildrens.org. Ronald V. title: Donald Trump v. Hillary Clinton is coming to the Supreme Court - MS NOW
content: The president said he wants to petition the justices in the 2016 election-related case. President Donald Trump wants to add another one of his personal cases to the Supreme Court’s docket: his bid to revive a lawsuit against Hillary Clinton and others, stemming from his complaint that ahead of the 2016 election, she conspired to “weave a false narrative” that his campaign colluded with Russia. A conservative appeals court upheld a ruling that rejected his suit and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against him and Alina Habba and her law firm. The appellate panel noted that “[m]any of Trump’s and Habba’s legal arguments were indeed frivolous.” Trump wants the justices to reverse that ruling. He said so in a filing seeking an extension of time to petition the high court. Justice Clarence Thomas, who fields such routine administrative requests from the circuit that ruled against Trump, granted the extension request Wednesday, giving the president until Sept. 9 to file his petition. It takes four justices to grant review of a petition. In the extension motion, Trump’s lawyers said his forthcoming petition will raise “exceptionally important” issues. They said the appellate ruling and imposition of sanctions “carries with it profound impact on the Presidency, and the nation as a whole.” This is only the latest of the president’s personal cases to hit the high court docket. Just this week, he filed his second petition seeking to reverse the millions of dollars in damages won by E. Jean Carroll, the writer he was found liable of sexually abusing and defaming. Last month, the justices declined to review an earlier petition he brought in a separate but related Carroll case, which he is attempting to get them to reconsider taking as well. Trump is also trying to get the justices to revive a defamation lawsuit he filed against CNN over the network’s use of the phrase “big lie” to describe his claims about the 2020 election. Like the 2016 election-related case, he’s been losing that 2020 election-related case at the hands of conservative judges in the lower courts and wants the high court to intervene. His petition in the CNN case is due Aug. 14 after his latest extension request, also granted by Thomas. Jordan Rubin is the Deadline: Legal Blog writer. He was a prosecutor for the New York County District Attorney’s Office in Manhattan and is the author of “Bizarro," a book about the secret war on synthetic drugs. Before he joined MS NOW, he was a legal reporter for Bloomberg Law.

title: Leslie v. City of New York Brief: NYC's "Suspect Index" of Secretly Harvested DNA Is Unconstitutional - Cato Institute
content: Sign up to have blog posts delivered straight to your inbox! When Appellant Shakira Leslie declined an offer of water seven hours after being arrested, jail officers insisted that “it would be some time before she had another opportunity to drink.” She took a sip from the disposable cup, then officers told her to “keep drinking.” They pulled her DNA from that cup, developed a profile from the sample, and entered it into New York City’s “Suspect Index.” Leslie is far from the only person on it. For more than a decade, New York City has been amassing the DNA samples of New Yorkers without their consent or any court involvement, as a routine matter, specifically for inclusion in its “Suspect Index,” a rogue database not authorized by law. Defendants regularly include samples from people who, as in this case, have been expressly excluded as suspects in a crime, as well as missing persons and their relatives, suspects who have never been charged with a crime, arrestees who have never been convicted of a crime, and exonerated or acquitted individuals. The Suspect Index currently contains 54,105 profiles, many from people who have never been convicted of, much less charged with or even suspected of, a crime. The New York Police Department’s (NYPD) collection methodologies for the Suspect Index have long been reported to be racially discriminatory. Further, the NYPD routinely collects DNA samples in an orchestrated surreptitious manner through ruses involving straws, bottles, or even cigarettes, without the knowledge or consent of the searched individual and without a court order. The NYPD harvests DNA not only from adults who are charged with crimes—it also surreptitiously takes DNA from those who are merely brought in for questioning and even from children it tricks. These DNA samples are then processed into profiles and entered into the Suspect Index without individuals’ knowledge, much less their consent. The consequences of having one’s DNA profile in the Suspect Index are enormous. The Suspect Index provides search capacity for half or more of all the criminal investigations in New York implicating DNA. And, because it is not subject to any statutory restrictions, it could be searched or shared for any number of purposes. Cato joined an amicus brief filed by the American Civil Liberties Union and New York Civil Liberties Union urging the Second Circuit to protect New Yorkers’ genetic privacy rights by holding that such collection, analysis, and indexing require a warrant. DNA contains some of a person’s most private and sensitive information—ancestry, family relationships, propensities for serious medical conditions, and more. When combined with other public data, it can expose previously unknown family histories of adoptions, misattributed paternity, early mortality, or substance abuse disorders. Because DNA reveals so much about every individual, collecting, analyzing, and indexing it constitutes a search under the Fourth Amendment. The government must therefore obtain a warrant for the practices challenged here. Upholding these practices would allow the defendants to continue expanding their DNA repository, constrained only by the size of the population of New Yorkers whose genetic information they can surreptitiously harvest. The law demands better from the government. Every weekday morning: independent analysis grounded in individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and peace.

The 2027 Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq-V with a native NACS charging port entered the US market. General Motors has just launched the configurator, revealing only slightly higher pricing than in the 2026 model year. The specs appear to be the same, so the primary changes are new exterior paint colors and minor changes to the interior/standard equipment. The Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq-V are mid-size premium crossover/SUVs, based on the GM BEV3 platform (Ultium), produced at the GM Spring Hill Assembly plant in Tennessee. Just like the 2026 model year, the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq is available with either a single-motor, rear-wheel drive (RWD) or dual-motor, all-wheel drive (AWD) powertrain. The performance-oriented Lyriq-V has only an AWD version, with much higher power and 0-60 mph acceleration in 3.3 seconds. There is a single battery pack for all versions, although we can separately list two onboard chargers (11.5 or 19.2 kW), as in the past they got different EPA range and energy consumption ratings. The base Cadillac Lyriq trim is Luxury. The higher-power charger is available as an option in the Premium Luxury trim. All versions of the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq feature a 102-kWh battery (400-volt class). The 2027 model year version is expected to get the same EPA Combined range as the outgoing 2026 model year: up to 326 miles. Thus, we have attached the chart with 2026 range numbers below. An interesting thing, but not unique to General Motors’ EV lineup, is that the optional higher-power charger (19.2 kW) decreases the range in some ratings, compared to the standard 11.5-kW charger. 2026 Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq-V: EPA range. (Image credit: State Of Charge) The EPA energy consumption ratings have not yet been published for the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq, but we can use the same numbers as for the 2026 model year. The Lyriq is expected to average 85-92 MPGe, or 2.5-2.7 miles/kWh (337-362 Wh/mile), including charging losses. The Lyriq-V consumes more energy, as it gets 80 MPGe, or 2.4 miles/kWh (387 Wh/mile), including charging losses. 2026 Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq-V: EPA energy consumption (including charging losses). (Image credit: State Of Charge) The 2027 Cadillac Lyriq features a NACS (SAE J3400) charging port for AC and DC charging. That’s an important change compared to the previous model years, which relied on the CCS1 charging port. The first Cadillacs with NACS were the 2026 Cadillac Optiq and Optiq-V. Most recently, Cadillac introduced the NACS-compatible 2027 Cadillac Vistiq. The model can directly access NACS charging points (AC and DC), including Superchargers (General Motors’ EVs gained access to the Tesla Supercharging network in September 2024). Access to CCS1 DC fast chargers is possible through a CCS1-to-NACS adapter. Similarly, the car can use SAE J1772 AC charging points with an AC adapter (J1772-to-NACS). The charging port is located on the front-left (driver’s side). The 2027 Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq-V feature an 11.5-kW onboard charger. Optionally, a 19.2-kW onboard charger is available for $1,480 in higher trims. To fully utilize the standard onboard charger, an 11.5-kW home charging station (up to 48 amps at 240 volts) installed on a 60-amp circuit will be required. For the higher-power charger, a 19.2 kW charging station (up to 80 amps at 240 volts) installed on a 100-amp circuit will be required. The 2027 Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq V come standard with a dual-voltage (120- and 240-volt) charging cable rated at up to 7.7 kW. DC fast charging is not a strong point of the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq-V, as we know from an in-depth analysis of the 2024 Cadillac Lyriq AWD. The new 2027 model year is expected to have the same DC fast-charging results as the 2026 model year, for which we have full data. According to the manufacturer, the 2026 model-year Lyriq family can replenish roughly 80 miles of range (depending on the version) in 10 minutes at up to 190 kW. That’s probably the best one can get. Additionally, the 10-80% SOC charging time is 40 minutes. In such time, the car can replenish some 200-230 miles. The average replenishment rate would be just 5.3-5.7 miles/minute for the regular Lyriq and 5.0 miles/minute for Lyriq-V, which is low for a premium brand. We guess the 2027 model year has the same charging speed, though this metric isn’t listed. 2026 Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq-V: Range replenishment rate during DC fast charging. (Image credit: State Of Charge) The prices of the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq are only slightly higher than before. The entry-level Luxury trim with RWD powertrain starts at an MSRP of $59,400. After including the destination fee of $1,795, the effective minimum cost is $61,195. The AWD version costs $3,500 more. The 2027 Cadillac Lyriq-V is substantially more expensive, starting at an MSRP of $78,700 ($80,495 including DST). 2027 Cadillac Lyriq and Lyriq-V: Prices and expected EPA range. (Image credit: State Of Charge) BC Hydro’s public charging network in British Columbia, Canada, is promised to more than triple, reaching 3,500 ports by 2035. title: SubCtech Demonstrates 50 KW Continuous Power In 600 V-Class AUV Battery System - Ocean News & Technology
content: SubCtech has successfully achieved a major technical milestone in the development of a high-voltage, high-discharge-rate battery and charger system for a customer-defined underwater platform. As part of the project “The Development of 600 V Nominal High Discharge Rate Battery & Charger for a Underwater Platform,” SubCtech was required to develop a battery system capable of delivering 50 kW of continuous power for a minimum of 45 minutes at an operating temperature of 35°C. The system features a nominal voltage of approximately 600 V and a nominal energy capacity of more than 40 kWh. During the electrical full-load test, that took place lately, the battery system successfully delivered the required 50 kW continuous power for more than 50 minutes. This exceeds the customer’s minimum requirement of 45 minutes by more than 11 percent. Most importantly, the full-load test was conducted at a constant load throughout the entire test duration, as specifically required by the customer. The system was not throttled or power-limited due to temperature-related constraints. This successful demonstration represents a significant milestone for SubCtech. The achievement marks the first time the company has demonstrated a continuous output of 50 kW from an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) battery system. At the same time, the project represents SubCtech’s successful entry into the 600 V-class battery segment. The project presented significant technical challenges. At the beginning of the development, SubCtech’s proven battery technology had already demonstrated continuous power levels of up to 35 kW. The new customer requirement, however, called for a substantial increase to 50 kW continuous power, combined with a nominal system voltage of approximately 600 V. Rather than relying on fundamentally new battery technologies, SubCtech’s engineering team achieved the required performance by further developing and optimizing the company’s established technology platform. The result demonstrates the capability of SubCtech’s battery architecture to scale to significantly higher voltage and power levels while maintaining the high standards required for demanding underwater applications. “For the first time, we have demonstrated the truly enormous performance of 50 kW continuous power from an AUV battery system. And we achieved this based on our proven technology, without having to introduce fundamentally new technologies,” says Stefan Marx, CEO. “The test even ran for more than 50 minutes instead of the required 45 minutes. Under these conditions, this is an outstanding result and a major achievement for the entire team.” The customer specifically required the battery to maintain its full electrical load continuously for the complete 45-minute test period. The system therefore had to deliver the required power without thermal throttling or a reduction in output caused by temperature-related limitations. The successful test confirmed that the battery system can maintain the required 50 kW continuous output under the defined operating conditions. The achievement is particularly significant in view of the demanding operating environment of underwater platforms, where high energy density, power capability, thermal management, reliability, and system integration must work together within a highly constrained system architecture. The project also demonstrates the value of SubCtech’s established battery technology and engineering expertise. The development did not require a complete technological departure from the company’s existing platform. Instead, the SubCtech team successfully leveraged its proven battery technology and engineering know-how to achieve a substantial increase in continuous power output and system voltage. This approach combines innovation with a high degree of technological maturity—an important factor for customers developing advanced underwater systems where reliability and predictable performance are critical. “But with the best team—and by that I mean everyone at SubCtech—we had absolute confidence that we could deliver. This result once again confirms our position as a leading global supplier of high-performance underwater battery systems,” said Stefan Marx. The successful full-load test marks an important development milestone, but the project continues. The next major step will be the Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) at SubCtech’s facilities. Following this, the system will undergo OSAT at the customer’s site in autumn. The development program also includes the qualification of the system against demanding environmental and electromagnetic requirements, including qualification testing in accordance with MIL-STD-810G and MIL-STD-461E/F, covering areas such as environmental robustness, shock and vibration, temperature, humidity, and electromagnetic compatibility. title: Pattie Gonia v. Patagonia: When Trademark Enforcement Becomes a Brand Crisis - JD Supra
content:
In this episode of The Upper Brand®, Mayer Brown IP partners Rich Assmus and Kristine Young examine the trademark dispute between Patagonia Inc., the $1.47 billion outdoor apparel company, and Wyn Wiley's drag persona, "Pattie Gonia," an environmental activist and content creator. They discuss how Patagonia's infringement suit triggered a public backlash and "Streisand effect," amplifying awareness of Pattie Gonia's name far beyond what organic use ever could have. The hosts unpack the legal merits, including Patagonia's duty to police its mark, the weakened parody defense after the Supreme Court's Jack Daniels v. VIP Products decision, and the complicating role of Patagonia's geographic origin. They also cover practical takeaways for practitioners, highlight that enforcement decisions are as much brand strategy decisions as legal ones, and underscore that coexistence agreements remain an underused alternative to litigation. title: I’m torn by the hard hat v graduation cap debate. Is it wrong that I want my kids to go to university? | Emma Brockes - The Guardian
content: As Andy Burnham intervenes, it’s clear that the shine is coming off higher education. But is society ready for this mindshift? Am I? For a while now I’ve been having a conversation with friends that a few years ago would’ve been largely unthinkable. Partly, this is because of how sheltered we all tend to be when trying to imagine our kids’ lives running on different tracks to our own. But it’s also about the world changing. A brilliant young person I know left school, took up an internship, turned it into a job and now she’s in her early 20s with no debt and a great position at a big fashion house. “Maybe I won’t go to university, either,” said one of my kids, eyeing me for a reaction, while I nodded thoughtfully and tried to ride out the panic. Andy Burnham’s announcement this week that university shouldn’t be the single, aspirational goal of all young people is perfectly timed and sensibly presented and shouldn’t sound as radical as it does. It is, of course, a correction to existing norms that university-for-all is a proper national goal and the only personal determinant of ambition and success. By contrast, Burnham said on Tuesday, this country should “value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap” as he spoke about tailoring technical and vocational training to meet local job needs and tackle youth unemployment. The evidence on the ground suggests that a culture shift is already under way and that Burnham is simply validating an existing trend. I’m in the US at the moment, where the cost-reward ratio of going to college is so out of whack that student numbers have been dropping for years. Smart people on podcasts direct young people towards their in-state universities, which charge a fraction of the cost of the prestigious private ones (not the Ivy Leagues, so much, which can afford to subsidise any family making less than $400,000 a year, but the smaller, boutique liberal arts colleges that charge as much as $80,000 in annual tuition and have been closing due to dwindling student numbers). In the UK, too, for the last two years, university numbers have dipped slightly. This is partly a result of changing demographics – smaller families mean a smaller supply of school-leaving 18-year-olds – and partly to do with the cost, as increasing numbers of universities charge the highest tariff rate, even those that, a few years ago, were middle to low fee-charging. The question is what this is doing to perceptions about the usefulness or otherwise of going to college, which, as we know, isn’t just about earning potential. In both the US and the UK, being a graduate still delivers average median earnings that are higher than the earnings of non-graduates. But while middle-class people make jokes about how their plumbers probably earn more than they do, the fact remains that it is the other stuff – the cultural and social capital of going to college – that underscores this particular bias. So it is that, while “low-value” degrees have been the target of derision for decades – ever since media studies became a thing in the 90s – when you dig down into why people want their kids to go to university, it has as much to do with social benefits as academic attainment. When will they meet the friends who will stay with them and godparent their children if not while sitting around watching mid-morning telly for three years as they slowly mature into adults? Are those friendships worth 10 grand a year? How, exactly, do you put a value on the non-academic stuff? I always think of a thing Don DeLillo said once about honouring a need to “drink coffee and look at the world” for a space of years, something that in the current economic climate sounds like a preposterous indulgence. And yet, for lots of 18-year-olds, it remains a valuable exercise. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more But not all of them. The problem with current thinking about university is that it’s so uniform, and the main takeaway from Burnham’s speech is a reminder that there is more than one way of doing things. You can go to college, or not go to college, or go at 35 not 18, and all those things should be regarded as equal. Meanwhile the whole conversation around college is just part of a larger one about changing work patterns in which, on the evidence so far, gen Z are proving reluctant to repeat the experience of their parents’ generation by taking up office jobs – with additional pushback from gen X, who feel they came of age in office structures that taught them all sorts of useful things, such as how to work alongside people they found basically unbearable. We all bring such biases to these questions of how to live life. I went to university and want my kids to do the same. My mum would’ve loved to have gone to university but had to leave school at 16 and I’m sure that’s in the mix, too. But when the question of college education came up in our house, I tried hard to take myself off generational autopilot, stop being so hidebound by precedent, and properly consider the alternative. Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist. She is the author of She Left Me The Gun: My Mother’s Life Before Me
