title: 1. FC Magdeburg v West Ham United | All You Need To Know - West Ham United
content:
1. FC Magdeburg v West Ham United
Pre-Season Match, Avnet Arena, Saturday 1 August 2026, 2.30pm CEST (1.30pm BST) West Ham United will draw the curtain on our 2026/27 pre-season campaign with a hotly-anticipated clash against German second-tier side 1. FC Magdeburg on Saturday afternoon. With little over a week to go until our competitive campaign gets underway, at home to Portsmouth in the Carabao Cup first round on Saturday 8 August, Nuno Espírito Santo and his team will be looking for a strong performance and result on foreign soil, as we look to fine-tune our season preparations. Certainly, we will be aiming to complete pre-season unbeaten, following a behind-closed-doors win over Colchester United and an emphatic 5-0 triumph over Stevenage, the latter of which came in between 1-1 and 0-0 draws at Southend United and Rangers respectively. Magdeburg are similarly set to bring their pre-season journey to an end this weekend, and are sure to provide a good test in front of what promises to be a passionate crowd, having won all of their summer games to date, too. A gripping encounter awaits then, and as kick-off looms you can find out everything you need to know by scrolling below... Tickets for Saturday's game remain on sale online HERE, priced as below: Seated
Adults €24, Concessions €22, 14 and Under €6 Standing
Adults €15, Concessions €13, 14 and Under €6 Concession tickets are available for school and university students, over-65s and supporters requiring accessible tickets. Supporters will be required to provide proof of eligibility at the entrance to Avnet Arena if purchasing concession tickets. Subject to availability, supporters can also purchase on matchday from 1pm CEST. There will be an extra charge of €2.50 per ticket for tickets bought at Avnet Arena on matchday. Magdeburg is not served by its own international airport. Instead, supporters will need to fly to either Leipzig/Halle Airport, situated 68 miles to the south east, or Hanover, situated 96 miles to the north west. British Airways fly direct from London Heathrow to Hanover, but there are currently no direct flights from London to Leipzig/Halle around the weekend of our visit. From Hanover, you can take a train or drive, either of which will take about two hours. From Magdeburg city centre, it will take 30 minutes to walk to Avnet Arena. Alternatively, you can take a tram, with lines 6 and 9 both taking you directly from the Central Station across the River Elber to the Arenen stop, which is ten minutes’ walk from the stadium. If you are driving, parking is available in car parks at the Avnet Arena and the nearby Messegelände fairgrounds. You can watch West Ham United's pre-season match at Magdeburg on our exclusive live stream on whufc.com! We’re streaming the action live to fans in the UK and across the world - and you can purchase your passes for just £5 by clicking HERE. 2026/27 Season Ticket Holders can watch the stream for FREE by logging into your account using your email address. Once you have logged in, please head to whufc.com/en/video/live-stream to watch. Should you have any issues, please contact Supporter Services. All the action from Germany can also be followed via our live blog on our website and app, which will commence approximately an hour before kick-off. Additionally, we will have a match report, highlights and exclusive reaction for you after the final whistle across our website, app and social media. Each member of West Ham United's squad will be itching for vital gametime in the team's final pre-season test of the summer, including our 2026 FIFA World Cup representatives El Hadji Malick Diouf, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Edson Álvarez, who are now back in full training at Rush Green. Tomáš Souček remains sidelined with the injury he sustained at the finals. Boss Nuno Espírito Santo waited until the 73rd minute to make any substitutions last time out at Rangers, so it will be interesting to see how he approaches the hotly-anticipated clash in Germany, a week before our first competitive encounter of the campaign against Portsmouth. The match also marks Magdeburg's last friendly game of the summer before they get their league season up and running against Eintracht Braunschweig, so their fans will be intrigued to see which players make the starting XI. Coaches Petrik Sander and Pascal Ibold have made a number of signings since the end of 2025/26, including Brighton & Hove Albion's South Korean youngster Yoon Do-young on loan, and Republic of Ireland youth international Anselmo García MacNulty on a permanent deal from Dutch outfit PEC Zwolle. Founded in December 1965, 1. FC Magdeburg were established when the football department of SC Magdeburg became an independent club as part of a reorganisation of elite football in East Germany. Just months after their formation, Magdeburg met West Ham United in the quarter-finals of the 1965/66 European Cup Winners' Cup. The Hammers, defending the trophy they had won the previous season, won the first leg 1-0 at the Boleyn Ground before drawing 1-1 in East Germany to progress 2-1 on aggregate. West Ham's defence of the trophy ended in the semi-finals, where we were beaten by eventual winners Borussia Dortmund. Magdeburg's first season as an independent club ended in relegation from the DDR-Oberliga, but they immediately returned to the top flight under Heinz Krügel, who would go on to oversee the most successful period in the club's history. Their golden era followed during the 1970s. Magdeburg won three DDR-Oberliga titles, in 1971/72, 1973/74 and 1974/75, while also lifting the FDGB-Pokal on three occasions, contributing to their record-equalling seven triumphs in the competition. Their greatest achievement came in May 1974, when an own-goal from Enrico Lanzi and a Wolfgang Seguin strike secured a 2-0 victory over holders AC Milan in the European Cup Winners' Cup final in Rotterdam. It remains the only major European trophy won by an East German club. Following German reunification in 1990, Magdeburg entered the unified German football league system. Like many clubs from the former East Germany, they found life more difficult in the professional era, spending much of the following three decades outside Germany's top two divisions. Their fortunes began to improve during the last decade. Promotion to the 3. Liga in 2015 was followed by a first-ever promotion to the 2. Bundesliga in 2018. Although relegated after a single season, they won the 3. Liga title in 2021/22 to secure a return to the second tier. The 2026/27 season will be Magdeburg's fifth consecutive campaign in the 2. Bundesliga, reflecting the progress they have made in recent years. Saturday's fixture at the Avnet Arena represents their final pre-season outing before the new league campaign begins at home to Eintracht Braunschweig on Saturday 8 August. They have impressed so far this summer and indeed will be eager to make it six wins from six against the Hammers. Saturday's hosts have conceded just one goal and scored 42, most notably securing a 23-0 win at amateur side FSV Havelberg 1911 in early July. West Ham United have not visited the Avnet Arena previously, but we did play 1. FC Magdeburg at Ernst Grube Stadium in the European Cup Winners’ Cup quarter-finals in March 1966. The Hammers had won 1-0 in the home leg in London, but were pegged back when forward Joachim Walter scored for the East Germans on 78 minutes to level the tie. However, John Sissons found the net a minute later to edge West Ham through 2-1 on aggregate. More recently, the Avnet Arena welcomed its record attendance for Magdeburg’s final game of the 2025/26 season, as 28,875 supporters watched the home side take on Kaiserslautern in 2. Bundesliga.

title: The V-10 Engine May Be Gone, But These Cars Will Never Be Forgotten - roadandtrack.com
content: We love a good V-10 engine, and these are the best of the bunch. New production cars that use V-10 power are no more. That train left with the departure of the Lamborghini Huracán and the Audi R8, which means this list is full of greatest hits from the past. Many are supercars, but there’s the occasional odd duck in the mix, too, including a few oddball SUVs and pickup trucks. These are the best V-10-powered cars ever made. The Viper may be dead now, but it’s the car we think of first when it comes to legendary, V-10-powered machines. The track-ready ACR version is a beast on the circuit, with a big 645-hp 8.4-liter V-10 and comically large aero. Prices for the ultra-barebones first-gen are still within reason, but the fifth-gen has skyrocketed in value since the Viper went out of production. No matter which version of the Lamborghini Huracán you prefer, you're getting a naturally aspirated 5.2-liter V-10 that shrieks its way to a high redline. This mid-engine Lamborghini has talents that span from the racetrack with the STO to excellence off-road with the Sterrato. Its successor, the hybrid Temerario, loses two cylinders and tacks on a couple of turbochargers. The Audi R8 was initially offered with a V-8, but not long after launching, it added a 5.2-liter V-10. Throughout its long production run, the R8 tended to follow the Lamborghini Huracán. We finally saw Audi’s incredible supercar go out of production after 2023 production concluded, but just like Lamborghini, Audi has a twin-turbo V-8 successor with its Nuvolari. Before the Huracán, the Gallardo held court as the entry-level Lambo supercar. This angular, mid-engine success story produced 493 horsepower and matured across 10 model years, birthing dozens of iterations and special editions. They’re still not cheap, but you can pick one up at the bottom of the market for around the $100,000 mark today. Read our 20-year retrospective review of the Gallardo The Porsche Carrera GT is one of the most special Porsches ever produced. You can trace its engine’s lineage back to Le Mans and F1 cars, which the sound should remind you of instantly. The 5.7-liter V-10 paired with a manual transmission is a combination for the ages, one its 918 successor even struggled to compete against. This particular Porsche is one of the greatest sports cars ever made in addition to being one of the greatest V-10s. WHY THE CARRERA GT IS STILL PORSCHE'S GREATEST SUPERCAR The LFA makes a strong argument for being the best-sounding car of all time. Lexus teamed up with Yamaha's musical instrument division, and they tuned the LFA's engine note like it was a guitar. Described by Toyota engineers as a "roar of an angel," we agree wholeheartedly. The 553 horsepower seems almost secondary. Almost. The LFA name is being revived for an EV to come in the future, but we’ll never forget this V-10 masterpiece. The E60-generation BMW M5 is perhaps one of the scarier used-car purchases one can make today, but that doesn’t make it any less tempting. Bellowing up to a redline of 8250 rpm, the 5.0-liter, F1-inspired V-10 in this M5 produced 500 horsepower and 380 lb-ft of torque. Its subtle and classy exterior makes this V-10-powered super sedan one hell of a sleeper. The M5 wasn't the only BMW M car to receive that magnificent 5.0-liter V-10. The big-boy, two-door M6 got the same engine, paired to either a seven-speed single-clutch automated manual or a traditional six-speed. Both are sure to cost you dearly to maintain, but it’s hard to complain too much after listening to its incredible soundtrack. In keeping the German super-sedan theme going, we present the Audi S8. It uses a 5.2-liter Lamborghini-related V-10 to haul its 4300-pound body to 60 mph in 4.8 seconds. The tuxedo-trim good looks and everyday usability made this car an excellent balance between work and play. If it wasn’t clear by now, you can tell the VW Group made good use of its V-10 from this era. The only pickup truck on this list is a banger. This is the Dodge Ram SRT-10, a two-door Ram with a wing and a gargantuan 8.3-liter naturally aspirated V-10 borrowed from the Viper. You could even get it with a manual transmission. It remains the ultimate performance truck to this day, but Ram is coming for its own crown with the Hellcat-powered Rumblebee launching next year. How cool is a diesel-powered V-10? Cool enough for U.S. emissions regulations to cancel the Touareg TDI's sales here (twice). Twin turbos aid the ten cylinders, and the engine produces 310 horsepower and 553 lb-ft of torque. Besides this Volkswagen, the only other V-10-powered SUV made was the Ford Excursion, making it an extremely rare breed. VW IS MULLING A NEW FLAGSHIP SUV FOR A MORE AFFLUENT CROWD The McLaren Solus GT is the by far the newest V-10-powered car on this list. It's a track-only special with a unique 5.2-liter engine that revs to 10,000 rpm and has 829 horsepower and 479 lb-ft of torque. Thanks to its slim single-seater design and carbon fiber monocoque, it weighs just 2205 pounds. It’s an absolute rocketship. title: Houthis v. Saudi Arabia: Round 2. This time it's regional. - Responsible Statecraft
content:
After fresh clashes with the Yemeni military group, Riyadh finds itself at the center of overlapping wars and skirmishes, including Iran and Iraq On July 28, Saudi air defenses shot down drones launched from Iraqi territory by “Iran-affiliated terrorist militias,” a Saudi ministry of defense statement read. The attacks targeted oil facilities in the Eastern Province and at the capital, Riyadh, itself. Days earlier, Houthi forces in Yemen said they had hit “sensitive” oil transport sites linking the Eastern Province to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu. Satellite images showed smoke over the kingdom's most important oil infrastructure. Both attacks come amid a wider escalation that began with the Houthis’ declared naval blockade of Saudi ports, followed by strikes on several ships and an exchange of missile fire with the kingdom. The Houthis say they will lift the blockade only once Saudi Arabia ends what they call a “blockade” on Yemen; they also have separate financial demands, chiefly, a demand for public-sector salaries and a share of the revenue from Yemen oil industry, which is located in territory held by the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government of Yemen. Saudi Arabia is now being squeezed from three directions in the widening U.S.-Iran war — Iraq to its northeast, Yemen to its southwest, and Iran to its east. (On July 18, Tehran struck Prince Sultan Air Base near Riyadh, its first direct hit on Saudi soil in nearly four months.) To understand why this matters beyond the price of oil, it helps to picture the crises as a set of nesting dolls. The innermost doll is Yemen’s own civil war: a decade-old fight between the Houthis (officially known as Ansar Allah), who rule the populous north from Sana’a, and Yemen’s internationally recognized government, formally led by a body called the Presidential Leadership Council. The roots of this war trace to the 2011 Arab Spring revolution, which toppled Yemen’s long-serving president and left a power vacuum the Houthis moved to fill, seizing Sana’a in 2014. Saudi Arabia and a coalition of partners intervened in 2015 with the explicit aim of reversing that takeover and restoring the internationally recognized government, and the war has continued in one form or another ever since. The middle doll is Saudi Arabia’s broader rivalry with Iran, a contest for regional leadership that has run since Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution, when Tehran’s new theocratic government began exporting a revolutionary, Shia-inflected challenge to the Gulf’s Sunni monarchies. Since the Houthis’ seizure of Sana’a in September 2014, Iran has absorbed the group into what it calls its “axis of resistance,” supplying it with weapons, funding and technical know-how, turning Yemen into an arena of proxy war between Tehran and Riyadh. The outer doll is the American-Iranian war itself, now in its sixth month, which has all but closed the Strait of Hormuz and pushed oil prices to record highs. This conflict set the other two into motion. Since March 2022, an unofficial truce kept Yemen’s civil war, the Houthi-Saudi war, and the Saudi-Iranian rivalry in Yemen quiet even as the outer dolls rattled. That calm helped pave the way for a Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023. What is new, and dangerous, is that all are now moving together. This month saw the fiercest clashes in years between Houthi fighters and government-aligned forces in the southern province of Dhale, which left dozens killed on both sides. Briefing reporters in Riyadh — where much of the official Yemeni government’s leadership operates — Yemen's new foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, said, “at the end of the day, we are prepared for any escalations.” She also warned that the “Houthis want to copy the Iran experience in Hormuz.” The trigger for current tensions was a July 3 Iranian Mahan Air flight, which landed in Houthi-held Sana’a to collect a delegation traveling to Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s funeral, the first such direct flight in more than a decade. Riyadh had long blocked exactly this kind of corridor, fearing it would be used to send weapons or military advisers to the Houthis. That fear proved well-founded, according to Reuters, which reported that the return flight on July 13th brought with it Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps personnel, along with missile and drone components. The Houthis have denied the accusations. Subscribe now to our weekly round-up and don't miss a beat with your favorite RS contributors and reporters, as well as staff analysis, opinion, and news promoting a positive, non-partisan vision of U.S. foreign policy. Yemen’s internationally recognized government, backed by the Saudi-led coalition, has always treated the country’s airspace as remaining under its own legal authority. When that plane returned on July 13th, the government struck the airport runway to stop it landing again. The aircraft diverted to Hodeidah instead. That strike was not a unilateral decision. According to Axios, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman personally sought and received President Trump’s backing for the operation in a phone call days beforehand. Riyadh, it appeared, knew it was gambling with the Houthi truce and risked inflaming the already tense standoff between the U.S. and Iran, and wanted American cover before it moved. The Houthis retaliated within hours, firing missiles at Abha Airport in southern Saudi Arabia, the first direct strike on the kingdom in four years. All of this demonstrates how entangled Yemen’s civil war has become with the wider U.S.-Iran war. Iranian officials made this connection explicit while the Houthi delegation was in Tehran for Khamenei’s funeral. Ali Akbar Velayati, the supreme leader’s adviser, told the group that the siege of Yemen “must end immediately.” Parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, praised Sana’a’s loyalty, stating that Ansar Allah “always stood by the resistance in defending Lebanon and Palestine.” Iran’s foreign ministry has stuck to a more measured public tone. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there is “no military solution to the issue of Yemen,” and the ministry spokesman called for the U.N.-brokered 2023 roadmap to be “fully implemented.” However, this diplomatic call quietly endorses the Houthi narrative. Both officials characterized Sana’a as being under "siege," and under “continued blockade,” a clear acceptance of the Houthi framing of Saudi restrictions. Saudi Arabia, notably, has not pointed blame at Iran directly for inflaming tensions in Yemen. Instead, Yemeni officials have leveled these accusations. Yemen’s information minister, Moammar al-Iryani, stated outright that Houthi military decisions are now “more closely tied to directives from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard.” Riyadh has let its own client government make the accusations it avoids voicing directly, perhaps because naming Iran directly would foreclose the diplomatic space Riyadh still wants to maintain. That restraint would fit a broader pattern: Saudi Arabia has reportedly been keen to see the U.S.-Iran tensions resolved diplomatically rather than militarily, having already rejected Washington’s request to use Saudi airspace and bases for Project Freedom, the U.S. plan to escort ships through Hormuz. Riyadh, in other words, is hedging on multiple fronts at once. It is avoiding a total rupture with Tehran even as it fights Tehran’s allies on its southern flank and in Iraq, where it conducted airstrikes on Iran-aligned groups with the U.S. on July 28. That hedging leaves the door to de-escalation narrowed, but not fully shut. Oman, the traditional backchannel in Yemen’s civil war, said on July 23 that it was coordinating with Saudi Arabia, “Yemeni parties,” and the U.N.’s special envoy for Yemen to try to revive the stalled political process. That same weekend, Omani officials were in Tehran running a parallel negotiation on the Strait of Hormuz, shuttling between Iranian and American positions on ship-routing and transit fees. Oman is, in effect, trying to broker both of the region's thorniest disputes at once — a measure of how much regional diplomacy now runs through Muscat, and of how intertwined the conflicts have become. But diplomacy is losing ground. Reuters reported last week that Western officials involved in the Yemen mediation are increasingly pessimistic about reaching a negotiated resolution. Meanwhile, Houthi rhetoric towards its Yemeni rivals and Riyadh has grown increasingly fiery, and Saudi Arabia has made clear that attacks on its territory and tankers won't go unanswered. Massad Boulos — Trump’s Africa and Middle East envoy who is also the father-in-law to Trump’s daughter, Tiffany — has focused much of his diplomatic work in recent months on Libya, criss-crossing the country to meet with members of Libya’s two rival governments in an attempt to secure a power-sharing arrangement between the two. Publicly, Trump’s team has billed this diplomatic effort as a worthy attempt to bring sustained peace and democracy to the country through the formation of a unified government that can put an end to 15 years of armed group violence and political factionalism. Back in 1975, reeling from the Arab Oil Embargo of 1973, President Gerald Ford signed the Energy Policy and Conservation Act. The law established the nation’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and framed it as a rainy day fund, made ready for the benefit of the American people should a crisis in supply reach us once more. Today, after two consecutive administrations, our rainy day fund has been drawn down to the lowest levels since 1983. Biden drew down 50 million barrels in response to COVID. The next year, he withdrew an additional 180 million barrels in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the largest release in SPR history, arguing that the move was needed to calm gasoline prices and cushion the shock from the war. Funeral services for Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly on July 11 at the age of 71, will take place on Tuesday in Washington and Wednesday in his home state of South Carolina. Graham was known as an astute conservative politician, a military hawk, and an ardent defender of Israel, which made him a polarizing figure in today’s political climate. Along with many world leaders, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid will be attending the memorial at the National Cathedral, according to reports. title: A Summer Al Fresco Afternoon at V. Sattui Winery in Napa Valley - San Francisco Bay Times
content: Driving north along Napa Valley’s Highway 29, you pass a plethora of imposing wineries with lengthy, winding driveways and majestic buildings situated in picture-perfect vineyards. Then you see it … a sprawling lawn dotted with smiling visitors at picnic tables, children running around laughing, and dogs frolicking in the grass. In the background is a beautiful old stone building surrounded by vines. You think to yourself, this spot looks fun. Turns out, you’re right. This joyous place is V. Sattui Winery. After a decades-long career visiting wineries around the globe, I rarely wax poetic and it takes something very special to inspire such rhapsodizing. My recent visit to V. Sattui in Napa Valley has me doing just that. I hadn’t been to the property in nearly 20 years. It’s a staple in Napa Valley, but I was always chasing the latest rising-star winery. I finally decided it was time to revisit this historic destination on its 50th anniversary landmark. Their story began in San Francisco where Italian immigrant, Vittorio Sattui, opened a small winery in 1885. Prohibition shut their doors but not their dreams. In 1975, Vittorio’s great-grandson, Dario Sattui, brought the family business back to life in Napa Valley with the goal of sharing the Italian lifestyle connecting wine, food, family, and friends. Stepping into their bustling, recently renovated market, Mercato del Gusto, is a feast for the senses. It’s sleek and modern, but you still feel like you’re in the old winery building. It smells delicious due to the numerous bar and food areas serving an extensive menu of sandwiches, cheeses, desserts, and more. At one tasting bar I spoke with a group of women celebrating birthdays, at another was a couple toasting their weekend away. The atmosphere was electric. It was there I met Tom Davies, the passionate, long-time President and Managing Partner of the winery. His love of V. Sattui comes shining through in his wide grin. “It’s not a job, it’s my life,” he has said. Along with Director of Winemaking, Jason Moravec, and Michelin-star Executive Estate Chef, Stefano Masanti, I was treated to an al fresco afternoon on the patio sampling award-winning wines, noshing on custom charcuterie platters, and even ending with house-crafted chocolates and gelato. To shine a light on V. Sattui’s commitment to accessibility for all wine lovers, they have started offering a free three-wine tasting flight every Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. In the current hyper-priced Napa Valley, this is a savvy move. Not only has it increased their business on typically slow tasting days, but it has also endeared itself even more to V. Sattui’s fans old and new. Because V. Sattui Winery was founded on the concept of sharing wine in the context of everyday life, the way to buy their wares is by visiting. As Tom Davies said to me, “Being direct it’s about the experience. In the old days, our tastings were held on a redwood board spread over two wine barrels. From the beginning, we wanted to make small lots of delicious wine and sell it directly to consumers.” V. Sattui’s roster of wine offerings is vast and includes recognized wines such as cabernet sauvignon, pinot noir, zinfandel, sauvignon blanc, and chardonnay, but they also produce limited bottlings of unique wines. Their lineup includes reds such as grenache, malbec, and petite sirah, along with whites ranging from albariño to sémillon, a variety of rieslings, and even sparkling and sweet wines. There’s always something new to discover. If you want to try the V. Sattui wines, you can buy them online (https://www.vsattui.com/), but I recommend visiting and getting the full experience. Bring an empty stomach and an appetite for palate-pleasing adventure with you! Here are two standout bottlings from my recent visit: 2022 V. Sattui Cabernet Franc, Alexander Valley, Sonoma County $80 As a fan of cabernet franc, I’m constantly on the lookout for new bottles of the classic variety. A centuries-old vine from the Bordeaux region of France, it’s one of the parents of the famed red grape, cabernet sauvignon (white grape sauvignon blanc being the other). V. Sattui’s expression showcases sultry aromas of dark fruits, tea leaves, and rose petals. Once you sip it, the earthy, savory notes are layered with a lush yet lovely texture. It is a beauty to drink now or to cellar for up to a decade. 2025 V. Sattui Chenin Blanc, Los Carneros, Napa Valley $38 Looking for a perfect white to quench your thirst regardless of season? This one is it. Chenin blanc is a grape known in France’s Loire Valley but also in a few pockets in California where it’s grown. V. Sattui’s vineyard in the cool Los Carneros growing area, straddling Napa and Sonoma, gives the vines plenty of time to ripen while maintaining acidity and freshness. Crisp and juicy with hints of citrus and orange blossom, it is alluring to smell and lip-smackingly good to drink. Pair it alongside grilled fish, roast chicken, or spicy curry. Author, speaker, wine consultant, and television host Leslie Sbrocco is known for her entertaining approach to wine and food. She has won multiple Emmy Awards for her work on PBS, which includes hosting the series “Check, Please! Bay Area,” which is now in its 21st season; “Check, Please! You Gotta Try This!” and the national series “100 Days, Drinks, Dishes & Destinations.” www.LeslieSbrocco.com

title: Rio Ngumoha goal settles Liverpool v Wrexham clash in New York - Liverpool FC
content: A late, deflected Rio Ngumoha goal helped Liverpool edge out Wrexham 1-0 in their pre-season fixture in New York on Wednesday evening. The 17-year-old had an effort take a ricochet inside the area that looped the ball over the goalkeeper and into the net with 15 minutes left, to settle the contest at Yankee Stadium in the Reds’ favour. It means Andoni Iraola’s side have won both outings on their USA tour so far, with a further match against Leeds United in Chicago to follow on Sunday. After the 4-2 victory over Sunderland in Iraola’s first game in charge in Nashville last weekend, the head coach made a handful of changes to the starting line-up, including berths for Milos Kerkez and Dominik Szoboszlai, with the latter wearing the captain’s armband. Liverpool could have taken the lead inside three minutes at Yankee Stadium. It was Szoboszlai who played a threaded pass into the path of Harvey Elliott in midfield, who in turn slipped Josh Abe in behind. The youngster’s effort was repelled by former Reds stopper Danny Ward, however. Shortly after, Lewis Koumas went early with a low shot across goal from just outside the area that didn’t evade the bottom corner by much at all. At the other end, Wrexham threatened when Sam Smith pounced on a ricochet inside the box, but saw his drive at close range deflect off Ifeanyi Ndukwe and spin over the crossbar. The forward was involved again when he got a touch to a bouncing ball from a long pass forward, which had Giorgi Mamardashvili advancing from his goalline. The ’keeper managed to get his body in the way of the ball to eliminate the danger. On 33 minutes, Koumas asked in vain for a penalty when he claimed he had been tripped by Dan Scarr after attempting to meet Szoboszlai’s through ball, but those appeals were waved away. Four changes were made by Iraola during the break, but Wrexham had an early chance as a cross to the back post from the left dropped for Ryan Longman, but he could only skew wide as he stretched to reach the ball. At the other end, tenacious play by Koumas kept a ball alive on the left before he found Elliott on the edge of the box. His swipe at goal was parried by Ward as it made its way towards the bottom corner. The goalkeeper was called into action again soon after, getting behind a crisp Szoboszlai touch and hit from just outside the area. A Nathan Broadhead thump from distance required a diving save from Mamardashvili as Wrexham threatened, but Liverpool took the lead with 15 minutes remaining. Szoboszlai rolled the ball to Ngumoha midway inside the opposition half. He ran at a back-peddling defensive line before arriving into the box, where a low shot took a deflection off Lewis Brunt and looped over substitute stopper Callum Burton. The Championship side spurned a late chance to grab a draw when Kieffer Moore scuffed over from Brunt’s delivery at point-blank range, ensuring it’s two from two for Liverpool so far on their tour of the USA. title: Cardinals' Masyn Winn drops brutal trade deadline quote ahead of game v. Cubs - Cubbies Crib
content: For much of the season, the St. Louis Cardinals defied the odds - and even after going 2-8 in their last 10, they're still on the edges of the wild-card race in the National League. Have they been good enough to change the plans of Chaim Bloom, who replaced longtime exec John Mozeliak last offseason? Definitely not. At least, not if you ask Cardinals shortstop Masyn Winn, who dropped a heater of a quote when speaking with the media during this week's series against the Chicago Cubs at Busch Stadium. "We could win every game for the rest of the year, and [Chaim Bloom] would still trade guys."Masyn Winn is expecting the Cardinals to sell. His fellow young veteran leaders are somewhat more circumspect. They all agree they share responsibility in how the post-deadline looks: I mean, he's not wrong. Bloom was brought in to bring back the annoying consistency the Redbirds embodied for much of the last three decades before falling on hard times in recent years. He's not going to let a decent first half overshadow the fact this roster is deeply flawed and far from being a legitimate contender. Dustin May and Ryne Stanek are among the names already being tossed around - and there could be a larger sell-off at hand, as well, depending on how far Bloom wants to go. As our friends at Redbird Rants point out, guys like Ivan Herrera, Alex Burleson, Lars Nootbaar, Kyle Leahy and Andre Pallante could also be shopped. As much as I'd love to bring in someone like Pallante or Leahy, there are no indications the Cubs and Cardinals are talking about coming together on a trade. Dustin May has been all over the place this year, but could draw interest as a depth piece for teams in need of arms. Yes, Jed Hoyer is looking for arms, but I don't think he's going to get one from St. Louis. That being said, if the Cardinals do end up selling, that could deepen the pool of pitchers available on the trade market - which might help Hoyer tackle the one job he's got ahead of Aug. 3: reinforce a staff that's battled and ground its way through injury after injury. So, while at first glance, this comment may not mean much to Cubs fans - it's worth taking note of. Plus, who doesn't love seeing your team's longtime hated rival caught up in some drama? Seaside: When client AI use can sink work product protection Massachusetts trial court holds that certain uses of AI to generate legal documents could compromise attorney work product protection. In its June 16, 2026, decision in Earl Wade Shealy Jr. v. Seaside Investments, LLC, No. 2684CV00799-BLS2, the Suffolk County Superior Court’s Business Litigation Session (Squires-Lee, J.) compelled production of documents that the plaintiff’s romantic partner had generated using ChatGPT. The court held that, on the facts before it, neither AI queries for legal assistance nor the resulting output were protected work product when made by someone who is not a party’s representative and not at the direction of counsel—even though the party was represented and the materials were created in anticipation of litigation. Although the trial court’s order is not binding on other courts, the decision offers an early and instructive window into how judges may treat AI-assisted materials in discovery. The dispute arose from alleged breaches of an agreement on the purchase and sale of a gas station in Boston’s South End neighborhood. The plaintiff, Earl Wade Shealy, Jr., alleges that the defendants defaulted on a promissory note and loan agreement by failing to pay as required under the agreements’ terms. Seaside Investments LLC responded by sending a letter to Shealy also alleging default. Shealy, in turn, forwarded the document to his partner, Debbi Fields. Fields then uploaded the documents to ChatGPT, generated a response letter and other documents using the AI tool, and emailed the output back to Shealy. No attorney was involved in Fields’s use of ChatGPT. Fields testified she was merely “like a Xerox,” assisting with “providing a paperwork flow.” Defendants moved to compel production of (i) the ChatGPT communications and output, and (ii) documents relating to Shealy’s financial ability to prepay the note. Plaintiffs argued that the AI-generated documents were prepared in anticipation of litigation and therefore were protected under the work product doctrine. The court’s decision turned on an analysis of three major requirements for the work product doctrine, which protects (1) documents and tangible things (2) prepared by or for another party or by or for that party’s representative (3) in anticipation of litigation or for trial. The court held that Fields, as Shealy’s romantic partner, was not a “representative” under the work product doctrine. The types of persons whose documents are protected under Mass. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(3), including a party’s “attorney, consultant, surety, indemnitor, insurer, or agent,” do not include a friend or partner with “absolutely no substantive connection to the litigation or to plaintiffs’ counsel.” Expanding the definition to cover such individuals, the court reasoned, would not “enhance the vitality of an adversary system” and would “expand the work product doctrine without meaningful limitation.” Plaintiffs cited two recent federal decisions—Morgan v. V2X, Inc., No. 25–CV–01991–SKC–MDB, at *2 (D. Colo. Mar. 30, 2026) and Warner v. Gilbarco, Inc., 820 F. Supp. 3d 629, 636 (E.D. Mich. 2026)—both of which held AI-generated materials are subject to work product protection. The court distinguished those cases because both involved pro se litigants using AI as both party and advocate. Here, plaintiffs were represented by “sophisticated, capable counsel.” The court found the case more akin to United States v. Heppner, 820 F. Supp. 3d 292 (S.D.N.Y. 2026), in which AI documents generated by a represented defendant on his own “volition” did not merit work product protection because they were not prepared at the “behest” of counsel and did not reflect “counsel’s strategy.” The court’s holding on this issue of first impression: Neither the queries of AI programs for legal assistance by a party’s romantic partner nor the AI output are protected from disclosure under the work product doctrine unless performed at the direction of counsel. The court further held that ChatGPT’s output does not qualify as opinion work product, which is discoverable only in extreme circumstances. As the court stated: “AI is a tool, not a person. Nothing about what ChatGPT produces discloses the ‘mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, or legal theories of an attorney or other representative of a party concerning the litigation.’” While Massachusetts courts have already confronted AI—most notably in sanctioning attorneys for citing fabricated, AI-generated cases (such as Judge Brian A. Davis’ 2024 warning to the “broader bar” in Smith v. Farwell, No. 2282CV01197 (Mass. Super. Ct. Feb. 12, 2024))—Shealy appears to be among the first to reach AI through the work product doctrine, and one of the earliest anywhere to do so involving a represented party. The court’s reasoning sends a strong signal: the work product shield may not extend to AI use by someone who is not a party’s “representative” and who is acting outside counsel’s oversight. Companies[1] and individuals would be well served to keep the following in mind: Route litigation-related AI use through counsel. The court’s favorable citation to United States v. Heppner is a strong signal that work product protection may turn on whether AI is used at the “direction of counsel.” Parties are well advised to involve counsel before using AI tools to draft or analyze litigation-related documents. Under the court’s reasoning, even a party’s own, self-initiated AI use could fall outside the doctrine’s protection. Think twice before sharing litigation documents with non-attorneys for AI analysis. Under Shealy, sending legal documents to a spouse, partner, family member, or friend who then uses AI to generate analysis, or draft responses may carry no privilege or work product protection. A close family relationship may not change the analysis: the marital privilege protects confidential communications between spouses, and the court’s reasoning suggests it may not reach documents a spouse creates by feeding materials into a public AI tool. Similar questions could arise as to parents, children, and other relatives, and the risk that such materials are ordered produced is a real one. Address AI use during disputes in internal policies. Organizations are well positioned to get ahead of this issue by making clear when employees should consult counsel before using AI tools to analyze or respond to legal matters, including demand letters, regulatory inquiries, and contracts in dispute. Revisit litigation hold and preservation procedures. Companies are well served to look at whether their litigation hold notices reach AI-generated content, and whether employees understand any obligations to preserve AI interactions relating to disputes, since opposing parties may seek their production. Favor counsel-directed or enterprise AI tools for litigation work. The decision is not a reason to avoid AI, but a strong reason to be deliberate about how it is used. Where counsel directs the AI use, or where the work runs through an enterprise platform with appropriate confidentiality and data-handling protections rather than a public chatbot, AI-assisted materials stand a far better chance of qualifying as protected work product. Since the President Trump began his second term, people, regardless of their immigration status, have faced relentless attacks for exercising their First Amendment rights. 13 of our affiliates’ clients were retaliated against for exercising their First Amendment rights across 5 states and Washington, D.C. The ACLU of New Jersey’s client was operating a mobile health clinic outside an ICE detention center where active protests were taking place inside and outside the facility — then she was attacked by ICE. Norma Bowe, is a grandmother, professor of public health at Kean University, and registered nurse who operates a mobile clinic that provides free medical services to people across northern New Jersey. Since May 2025, her clinic has regularly stationed at Delaney Hall to support families visiting loved ones in the detention center. “ICE agents are acting like they have impunity and are inflicting harm however and whenever they want; without accountability, more people will get hurt and die. ICE must be held responsible.” - Dr. Norma Bowe Throughout the protests related to the detainees’ hunger strike, she was operating her mobile health clinic. One day, an ICE agent grabbed Norma and violently threw her to the ground. ICE is incarcerating people in dangerous facilities, where people detained are subjected to systematic abuse and egregious medical neglect. Right now, there are a record 65,000+ people in ICE detention facilities nationwide as the Trump administration rushes to expand the ICE detention machine fueled by the for-profit private prison industry. For decades, ICE detention has been notorious for horrific rights violations, medical abuse, and utter disregard for the dignity of people in custody. 14 of our affiliates’ clients experienced abuses in ICE detention, and their stories are only the tip of the iceberg. Two of the ACLU of Louisiana’s clients were denied access to medication, forced into physical labor, subject to severe physical and sexual abuse, and retaliated against, including by being placed in solitary confinement. Mario Garcia-Valenzuela and Luis Renteria Gonzalez were detained for nearly two and three years, respectively, at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana. They suffered forced labor, physical abuse, sexual abuse, inadequate medical care, and severe retaliation by the facility’s staff, including placement in solitary confinement. “I’m speaking out now because ICE needs to be held accountable for what happened to me. And because I don't want this to happen to anyone else.” - Luis Renteria-Gonzalez As trans men, Mario and Luis were forced to perform intense manual labor in an off-the-books program that targeted transgender and masculine-presenting LGBTQ+ detained people. They were assaulted by officers and suffered serious injuries from forced labor. When Luis and Mario filed complaints about this abuse, they were held in solitary confinement for weeks, where they were denied food and access to their attorney. Mario was repeatedly denied his seizure medication, causing him to have at least 10 seizures in a one-month period, leading to his hospitalization. They both also experienced and witnessed sexual assault and harassment, including being forced to stand guard while an officer raped a detained woman. And when their families came to visit them in detention, officers stalked their families in the nearby town. ICE and federal law enforcement are racially profiling and arresting U.S. citizens unlawfully. Federal agents’ actions have not only harmed people without permanent legal status, but also U.S. citizens. In fact, more than half of our affiliates’ clients (29) were U.S. citizens harmed by federal law enforcement — and of those, 12 U.S. citizen clients were racially profiled and unlawfully detained. One of the ACLU of North Carolina’s clients, a U.S. citizen, was racially profiled and put into a unmarked SUV before federal agents released him, bleeding, on the side of the road. Willy Wender Aceituno, a U.S. citizen in North Carolina, was on his way into a restaurant when four armed and masked immigration agents surrounded him, pushed him against an agency’s vehicle, and forced him to provide identification to confirm his citizenship. Mr. Aceituno provided his Real ID driver’s license, and after confirming his citizenship, the agents walked away. But moments later after returning to his truck, agency vehicles pulled in front and behind him to block his exit. While he began to record, the agents shattered his window and attempted to grab his phone before holding Mr. Aceituno in a headlock and pulling him from his truck. He was thrown onto the pavement, which was covered in broken glass, and he suffered bleeding cuts all over his body. Mr. Aceituno was handcuffed, placed in an unmarked SUV, and driven away from the scene. He kept repeating that he was a citizen while the agents continued to tell him to “shut up.” Eventually, the SUV stopped, an agent took Mr. Aceituno’s wallet from his front pocket and confirmed that he was a citizen with no criminal record. The agents released Mr. Aceituno on the side of the road, still bleeding and 2 miles away from his truck. As these stories show, federal agents’ abuses are not limited to any one population, demographic, or surge. The ACLU’s new report, Agents of Chaos and Cruelty, underscores how federal agents' conduct has harmed citizens and noncitizens alike in states across the country. The report examines immigration enforcement incidents in eight states and found that over 400 of the more than 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents examined involved misconduct by immigration agents. Though the incidents examined represent a small fraction of total reported enforcement activity in 2025, the pattern across eight states makes clear that excessive force, racial profiling, intimidation, and abuse by both federal officials and state and local law enforcement are paramount to the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant agenda.

title: King v. United States – Challenging National Guard Members’ Violent Seizure of a Veteran - ACLU of DC
content: Anna King is a retired U.S. Army captain and an Iraq War veteran, receiving a Purple Heart and a Bronze Star for her service. On May 8, 2026, she was at her home when three National Guard members walked through her gated patio and seized her, shoving her toward the ground, grabbing her arms, and applying handcuffs so tightly that they ruptured ligaments in her wrist, requiring surgery. The Guard members contended that they detained King because she assaulted them two days earlier; but this assertion is baseless and King was never charged with the alleged offense. Instead, the only apparent reason for the Guard members’ decision to target her was her speech, via the prominent signs in her window criticizing their presence in the District. In conjunction with the law firm Levy Firestone Muse LLP, we filed an administrative Federal Tort Claims Act complaint with the Idaho National Guard (which employs several of the Guard members involved) and the Department of Defense to vindicate King’s rights. title: Magnachip licenses Navitas’s GeneSiC silicon carbide technology for 1,200 V and above - Charged EVs
content: Posted July 29, 2026 by Chris Ruoff & filed under Newswire, The Tech. Magnachip Semiconductor is moving into the high-voltage and ultra-high-voltage silicon carbide market by licensing Navitas Semiconductor’s GeneSiC technology. The license covers Navitas’ Gen 4 and Gen 5 GeneSiC Trench-Assisted Planar (TAP) technologies at 1,200 V, 2,300 V, 3,300 V and higher. GeneSiC came to Navitas through its August 2022 acquisition of GeneSiC Semiconductor. Charged covered the Gen 5 platform when Navitas introduced it in February 2026. The TAP structure is the basis of Navitas’s high-voltage SiC devices for medium-voltage grid and infrastructure applications. Magnachip also gains access to Navitas’s SiC supply chain and materials ecosystem. The technology is planned to be ported, qualified and internalized at Magnachip’s fab in South Korea, and the companies expect that approach to speed Magnachip’s entry into SiC while maintaining continuity with Navitas’ existing technology and materials base. The companies say the licensed technologies will support applications including energy and grid infrastructure, energy storage, industrial electrification, automotive and other high-power systems in Korea. Navitas and Magnachip say the agreement also covers areas beyond SiC that they expect to detail later. “By licensing our proven GeneSiC technologies and supporting Magnachip through our supply-chain and materials ecosystem, we are creating a path to scale advanced SiC solutions more rapidly while enabling a deeper, long-term collaboration between our companies,” said Chris Allexandre, Navitas President and CEO. At 3,300 V and above, SiC devices compete with silicon IGBTs in grid-scale converters and traction drives. A higher blocking voltage per device reduces the number of parts that have to be connected in series, and SiC’s lower switching losses allow higher switching frequencies and smaller magnetics. “This agreement opens an important new market opportunity for Magnachip in high-voltage and ultra-high-voltage SiC,” said Chae Lee, Magnachip’s Chief Executive Officer. “The addition of GeneSiC technology complements our existing MOSFET and power semiconductor portfolio and positions Magnachip to serve customers that require higher efficiency, higher voltage capability and more reliable power conversion solutions.” The free webinar sessions from our Spring Virtual Conference are now available to view on-demand. title: Between stadiums, BTS' V turns to a book on quiet power of everyday life - koreaherald.com

Updated : July 29, 2026 - 10:43:29 Between stadium performances and global commitments, BTS' V has drawn attention to a book that explores the quiet power of simply getting through everyday life. Late Thursday night, the singer shared on his Instagram story "The Sensibility of an Everyday Person" (a literal translation of the Korean title), a newly published essay collection by the celebrated Korean lyricist Kim Eana. The publisher, Storyseller, said messages poured in almost immediately after V shared the book. "Seeing the response the moment V shared the book reminded us just how much it means to authors and publishers when an artist introduces the books that have inspired them," the publisher wrote on social media. Kim reposted V's story on Instagram with a brief note of thanks addressed to the singer by his given name, Kim Tae-hyung. One of South Korea's most influential lyricists, Kim Eana has written some of modern K-pop's defining songs, including Park Hyo-shin's poignant ballad "Breath," Brown Eyed Girls' era-defining dance hit "Abracadabra," IU's breakthrough anthem "Good Day" and Ive's self-affirming chart-topper "I Am." If self-help books often promise reinvention, Kim's latest collection argues for something more modest: returning to the rhythms of everyday life. Kim described the book as an exploration of "the small things that saved me when everyday life felt close enough to touch but somehow remained out of reach, when life seemed ever so slightly out of alignment and I felt alone in it." Kim turns her attention to those quietly sustaining an ordinary life. The essays offer comfort to readers who are simply trying to get through each day. "The days that unfold without dramatic highs or lows, without straying from their course, are proof that we're living earnestly," she writes. "How much time and effort does it take to simply keep that going?" Kim writes that finding happiness in such ordinary things is "a tremendous blessing." While everyone naturally strives for a better material life, the quality of that life ultimately depends on whether we have "small moments of happiness we can savor like pieces of candy along the way." The new collection is her first book in six years, following her 2020 bestseller "Ordinary Words," which has sold more than 200,000 copies. V's recommendation arrives as BTS enters another busy stretch. After wrapping up the European leg of its "Arirang" world tour, the group is set to begin performances across North and South America on Aug. 1. title: The Wistar Institute Receives Grant from V Foundation for Cancer Research to Advance Melanoma Studies | Newswise - Newswise
content: Browse experts available to comment on breaking news Request an expert contact, get responses directly to your inbox Find an expert by topic in a comprehensive database Newswise — PHILADELPHIA — (WEDNESDAY, JULY 29, 2026) — The Wistar Institute, an international biomedical research leader in cancer, immunology, and infectious disease, has received an $800,000 translational grant from the V Foundation for Cancer Research. The grant, part of the V Foundation’s Breaking Barriers in Cancer Research Award program, will allow Jessie Villanueva, Ph.D., and her lab to pursue research into new potential ways to treat drug-resistant melanoma. Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, and cases continue to rise. While current treatments help many of those fighting melanoma, approximately 50% of patients do not respond to treatments. “This translational grant helps support our efforts to make targeted therapy and immunotherapy work better,” explains Villanueva, associate professor in the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program of the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center, and member, Melanoma Research Center, at The Wistar Institute,. “Our goal is to find treatments that either fully remove tumors or keep them away for as long as possible. By going after the cells that survive treatment, we hope to improve outcomes for people with melanoma.”Villanueva’s lab focuses on melanoma with mutations in the NRAS gene, a particularly aggressive and treatment-resistant form of cancer that is found in about one-fourth of patients. Until recently, there were few treatments for these tumors. Villanueva and her team have identified a key vulnerability in treatment resistant melanoma cells harboring mutations in NRAS—one that may be targeted by disrupting how these cells process fats and manage stress. By testing promising drug combinations, including some using existing FDA-approved therapies, the lab aims at stopping resistant cells earlier and help create longer-lasting responses for people with melanoma. “I’m truly thankful to the V Foundation for their support of this important project,” said Villanueva. “Although we focus on melanoma, this research has broader implications and some of our findings could also help improve treatment for other types of cancer driven by mutant RAS.” The V Foundation for Cancer Research was founded in 1993 by the late Jim Valvano, legendary North Carolina State University basketball coach, ESPN commentator and member of the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame. The V Foundation has funded over $500 million in game-changing cancer research grants in North America through a competitive process strictly supervised by a world-class Scientific Advisory Committee. Because the V Foundation has an endowment to cover administrative expenses, 100% of direct donations are awarded to cancer research and programs. The V team is committed to funding the best scientists to accelerate a Victory Over Cancer and save lives. The Wistar Institute is the nation’s first independent nonprofit institution devoted exclusively to foundational biomedical research and training. Since 1972, the Institute has held National Cancer Institute (NCI)-designated Cancer Center status. Through a culture and commitment to biomedical collaboration and innovation, Wistar science leads to breakthrough early-stage discoveries and life science sector start-ups. Wistar scientists are dedicated to solving some of the world’s most challenging problems in the field of cancer and immunology, advancing human health through early-stage discovery and training the next generation of biomedical researchers. wistar.org. title: Amicus Brief: Clemente Properties v. Pierluisi-Urrutia - Manhattan Institute
content: Don't miss the newsletters from MI and City Journal Roberto Clemente’s sons and their companies have spent decades protecting the baseball legend’s name, image, and trademark. In 2021, however, Puerto Rico enacted laws requiring motorists to pay for license plates and registration tags bearing Clemente’s mark. The program generated roughly $15 million for a government fund, despite the family’s objections and without paying compensation. The Clementes sued under the Lanham Act—the federal trademark law—and the Fifth Amendment. The First Circuit allowed some trademark claims against individual officials to proceed but dismissed the takings claim, holding that the Supreme Court’s categorical—or per se—takings rules don’t apply to “intangible” property. It also held that Puerto Rico enjoys state-like sovereign immunity which the Lanham Act didn’t abrogate. Now on petition for Supreme Court review, the Manhattan Institute and the Instituto de Libertad Económica para Puerto Rico (the commonwealth’s free-market think tank) have filed an amicus brief supporting the Clementes. We argue that a trademark’s essential property right is the power to exclude unauthorized commercial use. When Puerto Rico placed the Clemente mark on government products, set a price, collected the money, and kept the proceeds, it appropriated that core right rather than merely regulating it. The First Circuit’s tangible-intangible distinction has no basis in the Fifth Amendment’s text, founding-era understandings, or longstanding precedent protecting franchises, patents, contracts, liens, and other incorporeal rights. It also threatens brands, trade secrets, data, goodwill, and other assets central to the modern economy. Although the brief takes no position on Puerto Rico’s ultimate immunity, it warns that the rulings below could leave owners with property rights that lack remedies when violated. The Court should hear the case and reaffirm that government must pay for what it takes—even when the property can’t be touched physically. title: Tested: The Gas-Powered 2026 Honda CR-V Has Good Vibes, but Is the Hybrid Better? - MotorTrend
content: Honda’s stalwart SUV is as good as you remember, but the hybrid version is arguably the better buy. We know why you’re here, so we won’t bury the lede: Yes, the Honda CR-V is, in just about every meaningful way, still the same cheerful compact SUV that has established itself as a go-to purchase over three decades and six generations. The 2026 Honda CR-V EX-L AWD tested here is the most well-equipped gas-only model, with a price that places it smack in the middle of the CR-V lineup, above the gasoline LX and EX and the least expensive hybrid, the Sport. We liked the CR-V EX-L a lot—but is it good enough to be your next daily driver? Can this gas-only iteration make a case for itself against its competition, not to mention the hybrid CR-V in the same showroom? Let’s dig in. We’ll start with the basics of the EX-L AWD. For $38,805 as tested, you get a 1.5-liter, 190-hp turbocharged four-cylinder engine, a CVT automatic, and optional AWD. Leather-trimmed seats, a power tailgate, parking sensors, low-speed braking capability, eight-speaker sound, and an auto-dimming rearview mirror round out the EX-L’s light-luxury features. It’s cheaper than the hybrid CR-V’s entry-level Sport trim, but only slightly, with their base MSRPs just a few hundred dollars apart. The CR-V lineup got a comprehensive redesign for the 2023 model year, which brought a refined shape and such niceties as 18-inch wheels and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto—but there’s not much you couldn’t get on, say, a decently optioned EX. Perhaps a look inward will reveal the EX-L’s value proposition. With its leather touches, the EX-L’s cabin is a bit nicer than lower-trim CR-Vs, but you won’t find yards of luxury materials or big infotainment screens here. Everything inside feels high quality, durable, and well assembled, though, and the 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen is perfectly adequate for tasks related to operating a motor vehicle and its basic functions. Its front-and-center placement on the dashboard keeps your head up and eyes in the general direction of the road, and its unique blend of hard buttons and touchscreen functionality works well. Likewise, the 10.2-inch driver display is, uh, somewhat spartan, with a couple of round, digitally rendered gauges and a small center readout for tracking things like cruise control status as its default state. It is customizable to a degree, but there’s just not enough room to change things up too much. We appreciate Honda’s resistance to unnecessarily large interfaces in the CR-V—in no small part, admittedly, because it necessitates old-school physical controls for basic functions like climate and audio, which we’re coming to regard as nonnegotiable. Honda Sensing, Honda’s suite of driver assists, is included in every CR-V. It provides pre-collision braking, throttle control, and steering functions, as well as lane keeping, adaptive cruise control with Traffic Jam Assist, adaptive headlights, parking sensors, and cross traffic monitoring, among many other features. We found the adaptive cruise and traffic jam functions especially useful, though several times we noted an uncomfortable abruptness to the system’s braking in traffic, which might make us think twice about using it a lot. We found nothing uncomfortable about the CR-V EX-L’s perforated-leather-trimmed seats, though. Both rows are roomy and supportive, with plenty of legroom for front and rear passengers. The EX-L gets four-way power front seats, and for 2026 both rows get charging capability, with a wireless phone charger, USB-A, and USB-C for the folks up front and two USB-C ports for the rear passengers. Cargo space is one place the gas-only CR-V may have the hybrids beat—because it doesn’t have the same drivetrain componentry to package, the gas variant enjoys 3 extra cubic feet behind the second row, for a total of 39.3. There’s plenty of cargo room with the rear seats up and quite a bit more when you fold them. With rear seats up or down, the CR-V EX-L’s cargo volume beats the Toyota RAV-4, Subaru Forester, and Nissan Rogue, too. Overall, the CR-V’s ergonomics and layout feel familiar, with controls that are thoughtfully laid out and excellent outward visibility—in short, all the things that make getting into a 2026 CR-V like slipping on an old sweater are in evidence. You’ll have to decide whether that’s a desirable quality or not. With a turbocharged, direct-injected 1.5-liter I-4 engine pushing 190 horsepower and 179 lb-ft of torque through a CVT automatic, the AWD CR-V EX-L went from 0 to 60 mph in 8.4 seconds in our testing, which makes it a tad slow for the broader segment. Notably, it’s also slower than it used to be. In 2026, the CR-V’s natural enemy, the Toyota RAV4, can get to 60 mph more than a second quicker at minimum, but with a big caveat to bear in mind: All RAV4s are now hybrids. A 2025 RAV4 with the now-retired gas powertrain needed around eight seconds, and the newly redesigned gas Mazda CX-5 needed 8.8 seconds to get to 60 mph in our testing. And the CR-V hybrid? It’s right on the RAV4, with a 0–60-mph time of about 7.5 seconds. All that being said, though, our gas CR-V didn’t feel especially slow. From a stop and when hitting the accelerator from low speeds, it exhibited little of the throttle lag or surging that often plagues vehicles with small turbocharged engines. It revs like a Honda should, but it does so linearly, smoothly, and without drama, in part thanks to its CVT transmission, which feels as much like a traditional automatic as you could reasonably expect. That’s only part of what makes the 2026 CR-V an unexpected pleasure to drive, though. Its brakes have surprisingly good feel for a vehicle of this kind, with decent bite and a pedal that accurately translates what’s going on at the wheels. Handling is similarly pleasing. The term “carlike” gets throw around a lot in regard to small SUVs, but in this case, it’s apt; the CR-V isn’t a canyon-carver, but we think its cornering, AWD grip, and general sense of composure and stability make it above average for the segment—even, dare we say, a little bit fun. Steering feel did leave something to be desired, though. Also leaving something to be desired is the gas CR-V’s fuel economy. We realized about 26 mpg average in our time with the SUV, good for a driving range in the neighborhood of 364 miles—significantly less than the official rating of 27/31/29 mpg city/highway/combined should yield. AWD doesn’t help matters, but as you’d expect, the hybrid variants trounce the gas CR-Vs in this regard, even when identically equipped—the most efficient AWD hybrid gets 40/34 mpg city/highway and 518 miles of range, and even the least efficient hybrid variant, the new TrailSport, gets 38/33 mpg and can go nearly 500 miles between fill-ups. If you’re thinking it sounds like the CR-V is behind the times, we can’t argue with you—but that may be one of its greatest selling points. It neither overwhelms nor underwhelms; it’s a totally familiar, even comforting experience while managing to offer some driver engagement. It’s easy to see what makes this vehicle the default for so many buyers, year after year. If you want the nicest gas-only 2026 CR-V you can get, you’ll find little to regret about the EX-L. If you’re looking for maximum value and the most traditional CR-V experience, though, the second-tier EX or even the base LX may offer enough for thousands less than the EX-L. And while we’re at it, unless you’re allergic to orange accents, we think the Sport Hybrid, which starts within a few hundred dollars of the EX-L but offers superior power and efficiency and comparable amenities, is worthy of serious consideration. Whatever flavor you choose, though, it’s tough to go wrong with a Honda CR-V. Get the newest car reviews, hottest auto news, and expert analysis of the latest trends delivered straight to your inbox! title: We Tested the Honda CR-V and the Mazda CX-5 to See Which Compact SUV Is Better - Car and Driver
content:
The CX-5 and CR-V are both longtime Car and Driver favorites, but with the Mazda fully redesigned for 2026, which one comes out on top? Let's make a bet. Head over to your well-lit display case (or back closet) stacked full of old Car and Driver issues, dust off any 10Best issue from the last decade or so, and we'd wager that either the Honda CR-V or Mazda CX-5 is on that list. With nine of the 10 most recent 10Best lists containing either the Honda or the Mazda, it's clear that the two models are perennial favorites around our office—and, according to sales figures, around the country. Since Mazda gave the CX-5 a full redesign for 2026, we figured it was a good time to get these two longtime favorites together for a bit of friendly competition. Much like a Burger King order, the 2026 Honda CR-V can be had your way. The lineup starts with the LX at $32,370, which is powered by a 190-hp turbocharged 1.5-liter inline-four, and is available in front- or all-wheel drive. If you're looking for a bit more power, a few more features, or better fuel economy, the CR-V's got you covered with an entire lineup of hybrids. We tested a 2026 EX-L, the top trim for nonhybrid CR-Vs, starting at $36,850; the all-wheel drive and optional Radiant Red Metallic paint push its as-tested price to $38,805. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V for sale and new 2026 Mazda CX-5 for sale near 82001 Currently, Mazda's CX-5 stable contains just one powertrain, although a hybrid model is slated to arrive for 2027. Every 2026 CX-5, including our Premium Plus test model, comes equipped with a 187-hp 2.5-liter inline-four, and all-wheel drive is standard. The CX-5's price band is a bit broader than the Honda's, starting at $31,485 and rising all the way to $40,485, with our test example coming in at $41,080 with its extra-cost Aero Gray Metallic paint. Whether you see Honda's interior design as a positive or a negative is up to you, but the fact is, the design works. The CR-V's interior is roomy and easy to see out of. The materials—at least in our EX-L—are high-quality and comfortable to the touch even if they don't impress much beyond that. The layout is simple, with 9.0 inches of infotainment screen acreage to provide you with what you need, but not enough to overwhelm. Climate controls are fuss-free. Want it warmer? Turn that obviously placed dial on the dashboard to the right. Is your butt a little cold? Don't worry, the heated seat button is placed well within arm's reach. Can't quite hear the music over the sound of your own singing? You've got physical controls on the steering wheel and infotainment screen ready to pump up the volume. HIGHS: Smart interior layout, hugely practical, confidence-inspiring dynamics. LOWS: Noisy cabin, lacks any premium feel, could be quicker. VERDICT: Easy to love, hard to hate. Mazda's interior, on the other hand, goes all in on digital controls. The new-generation CX-5 places just about every non-driving function, from volume to vehicle settings, on the 15.6-inch dash-mounted do-it-all touchscreen. So long as you're cool with this approach, the CX-5's interior impresses. The seats, doors, and dashboard all sport leather wrappings, and the new "Mazda" script on the steering wheel evokes thoughts of luxury goods. Sitting in the CX-5, you're met with a cozy space that feels more premium than what's in the Honda, but we can't help noticing that the refreshed car doesn't seem quite as upscale as the older version. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V for sale and new 2026 Mazda CX-5 for sale near 82001 The CR-V's airy cabin puts a premium on passenger space and narrowly edges the CX-5 in rear-seat room—this despite the Honda having a shorter wheelbase: 106.3 inches to the Mazda's 110.8. In compact SUVs, storage space is as important as passenger comfort, and the CR-V wins there as well, offering 39 cubic feet behind the rear seats and 77 cubic feet with the seats folded. The CX-5 has 34 cubic feet behind the rear seats and only improves to 67 cubic feet with the rear seats laid flat. From an exterior-design perspective, we prefer the CX-5. Both models are reasonably handsome, but the Mazda's muscular lines and swoopy roofline evoke a bit more emotion, while the CR-V's aging design feels a tad more mundane. Should the two ever enter a drag race together, the result would be close. Despite the CX-5's extra 262 pounds, its 8.3-second run to 60 mph matches that of the lighter CR-V. The Mazda noses ahead in the quarter-mile, beating the Honda by 0.1 second, although the CR-V's 3-mph-higher trap speed shows the Honda is pulling harder by the end. That continues beyond the quarter-mile, where the CR-V reaches 100 mph 2.4 seconds sooner than the CX-5. Champagne for the winner, even if it is by the slimmest of margins. HIGHS: Superior ride quality, quieter cruising, more stylish looks. LOWS: "Everything's computer," ho-hum fuel economy, higher price. VERDICT: Still great but slips a little with this redesign. Honda did an admirable job tuning the CR-V's continuously variable automatic transmission to reduce that tech's worst attributes, but nothing beats the real thing, which is what you get in the Mazda. Urge the CX-5 to accelerate for a pass on the highway, and the six-speed automatic transmission kicks down to provide extra power for the task. And against the stopwatch, the Mazda beat the Honda in our 50-to-70-mph highway passing test by two-tenths. Despite that, the CR-V feels reasonably peppy. Give the throttle a good stab, and the Honda responds. Tell the CX-5 to accelerate, and it's got a hair more urgency than the CR-V, although the engine feels and sounds a bit less refined in doing so. The CR-V's small-displacement engine is efficient, earning EPA estimates of 27 mpg in the city and 31 mpg on the highway. That beats the CX-5's numbers, which are 24 mpg in the city and 30 mpg on the highway. Our test CR-V's observed fuel economy came in at 25 mpg; we don't yet have results for the CX-5 in that same test. At a steady 70 mph, the Mazda is noticeably quieter than the Honda. The former measures at just 23 sones, while the latter lets in more wind and road noise at 26 sones, or some 13 percent louder. However, the Mazda's coarse powertrain is more vocal under acceleration, measuring at 77 decibels to the Honda's 74 at wide-open throttle. Still, settle into a cruise on the highway, and either cabin becomes a quiet enough place to happily spend your commute. Leave your daily drive behind, and both cars are considerably more athletic than they need to be. The CR-V drives like most Hondas, with nicely weighted steering that has a solid on-center feel. The Honda has a touch more body roll than the Mazda, but unless you're driving them back to back, you'd be hard-pressed to notice the difference. The CX-5 is similarly dynamic. The steering has more of an artificial feel than the Honda's, but it provides confidence-inspiring feedback and a clear sense of on-center. We prefer the CX-5's softer ride to the CR-V's slightly stiffer one. Neither beats you up over bumps, but the Honda jolts you a bit more, especially over sharp impacts. The CR-V takes the crown thanks mostly to its easier-to-use interior, additional usable space, and its lower price. That's not to say the CX-5 isn't a contender. It's got solid dynamics, and it looks great—as long as you don't mind the screen-centric interior design. Furthermore, the Honda's more efficient powertrain and lower starting price make the CR-V the thriftier option up front and going forward. And in this segment, practicality counts. title: Before the Sensor: Filter Ordering and Self-Collision in Amsted Rail v. Squires - Patently-O
content:
The Federal Circuit has affirmed the cancellation of claims in Amsted Rail's railcar monitoring patent, along with the Board's refusal to let Amsted swap in substitute claims. Amsted Rail Co. v. Squires, No. 2025-1063 (Fed. Cir. July 24, 2026) (nonprecedential). U.S. Patent No. 10,137,915 covers sensor nodes and radios bolted onto freight cars to watch for derailments, damaged wheels, and overheating bearings. Claim 1 recites: ... (b) one or more sensors ... configured to measure accelerations of the railcar; and
(c) one or more filters configured to filter at least a portion of the accelerations ... Amsted argued the two elements as a sequence: measure first, filter second. But the panel held that the claim imposes no order, which opened the door to invalidating prior art. Both appeals were argued on June 1: this one and a companion covering two more Amsted patents, which the same panel disposed of on June 3 with a one word Rule 36 judgment. Ordering. A claim does not require its elements to operate in sequence unless the language, as a matter of logic or grammar, demands it, or unless the specification makes the sequence part of the invention. Amsted's hook was the definite article: claim 1's filters filter "the accelerations," which Amsted said refers back to the accelerations measured by the sensors. But the Board read "the accelerations" as including physical motion of the railcar rather than the signal alone, and the panel agreed. On that reading a silicone pad that keeps unwanted frequencies from ever reaching the accelerometer is filtering accelerations in the sense claim 1 uses.
